**"The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise"**: they will call out, begging. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said one of them will call to his father or his brother: "I am burning, pour some water on me!"

**"“Aid us with some water"**: literally "pour on us some water".

**"or any provision Allah has granted you.”"** As-Suddī said, "That is food." Others say it means the fruits of Paradise, or some of the food Allah has given them.

**"They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers"**: the believers will be told to answer, and they will say that Allah has prohibited both. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said this means the food and drink of Paradise, its water and its fruits. They are forbidden to the disbelievers because of their disbelief. The people of Paradise will not help anyone in what Allah has forbidden them.

### Why can't the people of the Fire enjoy Paradise's food?

The world offers two kinds of food, one worldly and one belonging to the next world. One kind of person feeds his soul on seeing himself made prominent. He is happiest when surrounded by worldly glory, and counts himself a success when he gains and owns worldly goods. He has forgotten Allah and the Hereafter completely. If anything about Allah is brought to his notice, he thinks it trivial and ignores it. He treats it lightly, as if it were not a serious matter but a game.

Such a person will have no share in the bounties of the Hereafter. He has raised a soul in himself that can feed only on worldly things, so how could the things of the Hereafter nourish it? Someone who did not live for the Hereafter in his life today cannot deserve Allah's blessings in it.

The other kind of person is absorbed in unseen realities. His soul delights in the remembrance of the Hereafter. His daily bread is living with Allah and breathing in the air of nearness to Him. For him the Hereafter will be a place where he finds every good thing he desires. He found Allah in the unseen world, and in the same way he will find Allah in the seen world of the Hereafter.

### In short

- The people of the Fire will beg the people of Paradise for water and food, and be refused.
- Allah has forbidden the food and drink of Paradise to the disbelievers because of their disbelief.
- A soul raised only on worldly pleasures has no capacity to enjoy the bounties of the Hereafter.

51.text:
The reply goes on to describe the disbelievers, and then Allah speaks: "those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.” ˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations.”" They are described by what they did in this life. They took religion as a game and were fooled by the world and its glitter, instead of working for the Hereafter as Allah commanded.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play"**: they treated their religion as sport and falsehood, as merriment, or as a joke and mockery. They used to mock and make fun of faith.

**"and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.”"** The comfort and luxury of this world fooled them. They were absorbed in its pleasures.

**"˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them"**: on the Day of Judgement. Others render it "We will forget them", meaning Allah will treat them as though He had forgotten them. Nothing escapes Allah's perfect watch, and He never forgets anything, as another verse says: "My Lord neither falters nor forgets ˹anything˺" (20:52). The word is used as a fitting repayment for what they did. Explanations of it differ.

- Al-ʿAwfī reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that Allah will forget the good about them, but not their evil.
- ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying, "We shall forsake them as they forsook the meeting of this Day of theirs."
- Mujāhid said, "We shall leave them in the Fire."
- As-Suddī said, "We shall leave them without any mercy, just as they left off doing anything for the meeting of this Day."

**"just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs"**: they forgot the meeting of this Day, giving up belief in it and neglecting the good deeds it called for, though they knew full well it would come.

**"and for rejecting Our revelations.”"** They denied Allah's signs, His scripture and His Messenger, even while knowing and recognising the truth of His message.

The same repayment appears in other verses: "They neglected Allah, so He neglected them" (9:67). "Just as Our revelations came to you and you neglected them, so Today you are neglected" (20:126). And: "This Day We will neglect you as you neglected the meeting of this Day of yours!" (45:34).

### A conversation on the Day of Resurrection

It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that Allah will question a servant on the Day of Resurrection. He will remind him that He gave him a spouse and honoured him. He made horses and camels serve him, and let him become a leader and a master. The servant will agree to all of it. Then Allah will ask whether he ever thought he would meet Him, and he will answer no. Allah will say, "Then today I forget you, as you forgot Me."

### Why do people forget Allah in His own world?

Allah makes His presence felt in the world through signs that a person grasps only by reflecting. Human beings lean toward what is outward and ignore the signs that point to Allah. But to do so is to give up the Hereafter for the sake of this world. A person who ignores the Hereafter while alive will find himself shut out of it after he dies.

When people show open disregard for something Allah has put before them as the truth, they are in effect treating Allah Himself as too unimportant to deserve serious attention. They may be fooled because the divine power behind the truth cannot be seen. Still, they run the risk of being ignored by Allah on the Day of Reckoning, just as they ignored Him in this life, imagining no harm could come of it.

### In short

- The disbelievers made a game of religion and were fooled by the comforts of the world.
- Allah never forgets, but on that Day He will treat them as forgotten and leave them in the Fire without mercy.
- This is a fitting repayment: they ignored the meeting with Him, so He will ignore them.
- People forget Allah because His signs need reflection while the world's glitter is easy to see.

52.text:
After describing the loss the idolaters will suffer, Allah makes clear that they have no excuse: "We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge—a guide and mercy for those who believe". He sent them the Book the Messenger ﷺ brought, set out in full detail. Since He has sent prophets and revealed books in this life, no one is left with an excuse.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have certainly brought them a Book"**: Allah sent the people of Makkah Muhammad ﷺ with the Qur'an. Another verse describes it: "˹This is˺ a Book whose verses are well perfected and then fully explained" (11:1).

**"which We explained"**: which We set out in detail and made clear, through tidings, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment. It explains and clarifies all things.

**"with knowledge"**: Allah has perfect knowledge of everything He explained in it. Another verse says, "He has sent it with His knowledge" (4:166). One explanation is "with knowledge from Us", and another is "We have taught it". Grammatically, "with knowledge" describes the state of the One who detailed it, knowing what He set out.

**"a guide and mercy"**: a guide away from error, to the right path and to the truth. A mercy that saves from punishment, because of the good it leads to in this world and the next. In the Arabic, "a guide" also describes the Book, through the pronoun attached to "We explained it".

**"for those who believe"**: for people who believe in it, in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an.

### Can anyone be punished without warning?

Allah says elsewhere, "And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺" (17:15). That is why this verse reminds the idolaters that a detailed Book has already reached them. Once the warning has come, no excuse remains.

### Why do some hear the Qur'an and others do not?

The Qur'an warns humanity of life after death and tells of the reckoning in the Hereafter, yet people do not wake up. Its warnings are not mere "news". They are the certain realities of the universe, which have not yet appeared as events and are still hidden behind the veil of the future. So the careless take them for empty talk and ignore them. But these messages come from Allah, who knows all.

People who have not spoiled their nature, whose eyes are not covered by artificial veils, find that the Qur'an speaks in tune with the voice of their own hearts. They find in it the very thing their nature was already looking for. For them the Qur'an becomes a treasure of life and faith.

### In short

- Allah sent a Book perfected and explained in detail, with full knowledge of all it contains.
- It is guidance and mercy for those who believe, leading to good in this world and the next.
- Since Allah punishes no one before sending a messenger, the idolaters who received the Qur'an are left without excuse.
- A sound nature recognises the Qur'an as the answer to what it was already seeking.

53.text:
The verse asks what the deniers are waiting for, and pictures the Day when the warnings come true: "Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺? The Day it will be fulfilled, those who ignored it before will say, “The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf? Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?” They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them". After refusing to believe, they have nothing left to wait for but the outcome of what the Book promised.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺?"** The question means: they are waiting for nothing but this. What are the people of Makkah waiting for, after refusing to believe? Only the outcome of what Allah promised them in the Qur'an. Mujāhid and several others said this refers to what they were promised: torment, punishment and the Fire, or Paradise. The disbelievers are warned of a painful punishment in the Hereafter, and the believers were also told of that Day's reward.

**"The Day it will be fulfilled"**: Ibn ʿAbbās said this is the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Judgement.

**"those who ignored it before will say"**: those who disregarded the Qur'an in this life, did not believe in it and did not live by what it required.

**"“The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth."** They brought the truth, beyond doubt, explaining the resurrection, Paradise and Hell, but we denied it all.

**"Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf?"** If only someone could plead for us now, so that we might be excused and spared the punishment.

**"Or can we be sent back"**: back to the first life, life on earth.

**"so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?”"** So that we may believe and do good deeds that would save us, instead of our evil and our idolatry. We would then affirm Allah's Oneness and stop associating partners with Him. The answer they will receive is "No!" Their wish is like the one in another passage:

> "If only you could see when they will be detained before the Fire! They will cry, “Oh! If only we could be sent back, we would never deny the signs of our Lord and we would ˹surely˺ be of the believers.” But no! ˹They only say this˺ because the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them. Even if they were to be sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. Indeed they are liars" (6:27-28).

**"They will have certainly ruined themselves"**: they destroyed themselves by entering the Fire forever. They lost Paradise and must stay in Hell, ending in perdition because of their disbelief.

**"and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them"**: what they worshipped falsely instead of Allah, claiming He had a partner, will abandon them. Those false gods will not intercede for them, help them or save them from their fate.

### What happens when the warning becomes real?

Those who do not take the Qur'an's warnings seriously will stay asleep until the event they were warned of breaks over them. Then a person will suddenly find himself completely helpless. The concerns he thought important, and was so caught up in, will turn out to be baseless. The things he relied on will be gone. The rosy hopes he lived on will all prove false.

Belief in the Hereafter seems to him an abstract idea now, so he does not take it seriously. But after death, when the Hereafter in all its terror is thrust upon him, everyone will be forced to accept what he once refused. He will realise that what he was told in the language of argument was absolute fact. Because he was not serious, he could not grasp its importance. When everything he relied on in the world deserts him, he will want to be sent back to earth to live properly. But no one is given that chance twice.

### In short

- The deniers have nothing left to wait for but the coming true of the Qur'an's warnings on the Day of Resurrection.
- On that Day they will admit the messengers told the truth, and wish for intercessors or a second chance.
- No return is granted. Even if they were sent back, they would go back to what they were forbidden.
- They will have ruined themselves, and the false gods they invented will abandon them.

54.text:
After the scenes of the Hereafter, the surah turns to the One who will bring it about: "Indeed your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne." The verse goes on: "He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession. He created the sun, the moon, and the stars—all subjected by His command." It ends: "The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺. Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds". The heavens, the earth, the planets and the stars all do their work within a firmly set order, and that points to a Maker of perfect power. Any reasonable person should then ask a question. If He could bring this vast universe out of nothing and keep it running by the wisest of systems, why would it be hard for Him to undo it all and create it again on the Day of Qiyāmah? The best course for people is to stop denying the Resurrection and to turn to that same Being as their Lord, their Master and Nurturer. They should ask Him for what they need and worship Him alone, and leave the swamp of worshipping beings like themselves.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed your Lord is Allah"**: O people, your Master and Nurturer is Allah.

**"Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days"**: He created the universe, the heavens and the earth and all that is in them, on them and between them, in six days, as several verses of the Qur'an state. He did it without any precedent. They ran from Sunday through to Friday. Friday is the day the whole of creation was gathered together, and the day Ādam was made.

Opinions differ on whether these days were like our ordinary days, as first comes to mind, or whether each day was a thousand years. The second view is reported from Mujāhid and Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and from Ibn ʿAbbās in aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's narration. They said the six days are six days of the Hereafter. One explanation says they were days from the beginning of this world's life, each equal to a thousand years. Another says they were days of this world in length, since there was no sun yet.

No creation took place on Saturday, the seventh day of the week. Its name, as-Sabt, means stopping or a break. Some scholars say the day was so named because the work of creation was complete by then. According to authentic narrations, the work of creation ended on Friday.

Imam Aḥmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the order of creation. Allah created the soil on Saturday, the mountains on Sunday, and the trees on Monday. He created unpleasant things on Tuesday and light on Wednesday, and on Thursday He spread living creatures across the earth. He created Ādam after ʿAṣr on Friday. Ādam was the last thing created, in the last hour of Friday, between ʿAṣr and nightfall.

**"then established Himself on the Throne."** Istawā followed by ʿalā literally means to take one's position on something, to settle or be established. ʿArsh means throne. In the classical language it is the raised seat on which a king sits. One explanation says, "He seated Himself on the Throne", and another, "then He proceeded to create the Throne". Others say He presided over the Throne in a way that befits Him, or established Himself on it in a manner suited to His majesty. The way to understand this phrase is set out below.

**"He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession."** He covers the day with the night and the night with the day. The verb can be read yughshī or yughashshī. Darkness departs with the coming of light, and light departs with the coming of darkness. Each pursues the other swiftly and is never late. When one vanishes the other arrives, and so on in turn. Another passage says:

> "There is also a sign for them in the night: We strip from it daylight, then—behold!—they are in darkness. The sun travels for its fixed term. That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing. As for the moon, We have ordained ˹precise˺ phases for it, until it ends up like an old, curved palm stalk. It is not for the sun to catch up with the moon, nor does the night outrun the day. Each is travelling in an orbit of their own" (36:37-40).

"Nor does the night outrun the day" (36:40) means the night follows the day in turn, arriving neither later nor earlier than it should. This alternation of night and day is a change on a revolutionary scale. It carries the whole world from light into darkness and from darkness into light. Yet it yields so swiftly, smoothly and obediently to Allah's overwhelming power that there is not the slightest delay.

**"He created the sun, the moon, and the stars—all subjected by His command."** All of them move in obedience to His will and command, under His dominion and by His leave and power. If the words for sun, moon and stars are read in the accusative, they are joined to "the heavens" as things He created. If read in the nominative, they begin a new sentence whose predicate is "subjected".

**"The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺."** To Him belong dominion and decision. Khalq means to create, and amr means to command. Being Creator and Master belongs to Him alone. No one else can create even the most insignificant thing. Nor does anyone have the right to put another under his command, unless Allah Himself entrusts someone with some area of authority, and then that too is really Allah's command. So the verse means that creating all these things was His work alone, and so was putting them into service. That too displays His perfect power. Is not the whole creation His? Who besides Him creates? One explanation takes "the creation" as the creation of the heavens and the earth, and "the command" as the judgement of people on the Day of Judgement.

**"Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds"**: this is like the verse "Blessed is the One Who has placed constellations in the sky" (25:61). Tabāraka comes from barakah, which means to increase, grow, abound, last and endure, besides many other shades of meaning. Here it means to be high and supreme. It can also be taken as high and everlasting, for Allah is both. The sense of "high" is confirmed by a phrase from a hadith: "You are blessed and exalted, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." There, "You are blessed" (tabārakta) is explained by the word that follows, "exalted" (taʿālayta). Others explain it as "the Possessor of grace", "far exalted is Allah", or "magnified be Allah". He is high above every flaw and has every attribute of splendour and perfection. He is the Lord of the worlds, their Master and Disposer.

Abū ad-Dardāʾ used to make a supplication that is also attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. In it he declared that all dominion and all praise belong to Allah, and that every affair is His. Then he asked Him for every kind of good and sought refuge with Him from every kind of evil.

### Why six days, when He could create in an instant?

Allah has immense power and could create the whole universe in a single moment. The Qur'an says so again and again. Sūrat al-Qamar says, "Our command is but a single word, done in the blink of an eye" (54:50). Sūrah Yā Sīn says, "All it takes, when He wills something ˹to be˺, is simply to say to it: “Be!” And it is" (36:82). Why, then, did the creation of the universe take six days?

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr answered that Allah is certainly able to create everything in a moment. But His wisdom required that the creation of our universe take six days, to teach human beings the lesson of working step by step and with care in running affairs. Another explanation agrees: an instant would have sufficed for Him, but He chose to teach His creatures caution and measure. A hadith supports this. The Prophet ﷺ said that acting with deliberation, dignity and patience is from Allah, and haste is from Shayṭān. Al-Baihaqī recorded it in Shuʿab al-Īmān.

The lesson is that rushing into things is not good for people. Someone driven by haste cannot think a matter through or weigh all its sides. A hasty act spoils the work and ends in regret. Whatever is done with forethought and at an easy pace brings barakah, the blessing from Allah that improves the effort and its result.

### How could there be days before the sun?

Day and night are known by the movement of the sun. Before the earth and the heavens existed, there was no sun or moon. So on what basis are six days counted?

For this reason some commentators said that six days means a span of time equal to six of our days and nights. A clearer approach is that our terms for day and night belong to this world. Day is what runs from sunrise to sunset, and night from sunset to the next sunrise. Before the universe existed, Allah may have set other signs for day and night. So it will be in Paradise, where day and night will not depend on the sun's movement.

This also shows that the six days in which the earth and heavens were created need not equal six of our days. They may have been longer, as the Qur'an says of a day of the Hereafter that it equals a thousand years. Abū ʿAbdullāh Rāzī said, as recorded in Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, that the farthest sphere moves so fast compared with our earth that a running man's raised foot has not yet touched the ground before that sphere has travelled three thousand miles.

### How were the six days divided?

The details of the six days come in Sūrah Ḥā Mīm as-Sajdah (Fuṣṣilat):

> "Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “How can you disbelieve in the One Who created the earth in two Days? And how can you set up equals with Him? That is the Lord of all worlds. He placed on the earth firm mountains, standing high, showered His blessings upon it, and ordained ˹all˺ its means of sustenance—totaling four Days exactly—for all who ask" (41:9-10).

The earth was created in two days. Then, in two more days, came the mountains, rivers and streams, trees and plants, and everything that humans and animals eat, making four days in all. The first two days, when the earth was created, were Sunday and Monday. The next two, when the mountains, rivers and the earth's means of life were created, were Tuesday and Wednesday. Then: "So He formed the heaven into seven heavens in two Days" (41:12). Those two days were Thursday and Friday. So by Friday the total came to six days.

### How should "established Himself on the Throne" be understood?

People have held many conflicting opinions about this phrase. The way followed here is that of the righteous predecessors. Among them are Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, ath-Thawrī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, ash-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh, and the rest of the scholars of Islam, past and present. They accept al-istawā as it appears. They do not discuss its inner nature, liken it to the attributes of creatures, distort it or deny it in any way. Whatever meaning occurs to those who liken Allah to His creation is rejected, for nothing resembles Allah: "There is nothing like Him, for He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing" (42:11).

The imams said the same. Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād al-Khuzāʿī, teacher of Imam al-Bukhārī, said that whoever likens Allah to His creation has committed kufr. Whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has also committed kufr. Nothing that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have said in describing Him involves any likeness to creation. Whoever affirms Allah's attributes as the clear verses and authentic hadiths state them, in a way that befits His majesty and denies Him every flaw, has taken the path of guidance.

The safest creed here, clear, correct and free of doubt, is that of the Companions and the Successors, and later of many Sufi thinkers too. Human reason cannot grasp the reality of Allah's Being and attributes. Chasing after its exact reality is futile, and even harmful. As a general principle one should believe that whatever meaning Allah intended is the true and correct one, and not try to fix a meaning of one's own.

Someone asked Imam Mālik exactly this question: what does "established Himself on the Throne" mean? He paused for a while and then answered. Everyone knows what istawā means, he said, but its particular nature and reality are beyond the reach of human reason. Believing in it is obligatory (wājib), and asking about its nature and reality is bidʿah, an innovation, because the noble Companions never asked the Prophet ﷺ such questions. The great early scholars (Salaf) said the same. They include Sufyān ath-Thawrī, Imam al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah and ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak. Verses about Allah's Being and attributes, they said, should be believed in just as they came, without explanation, elaboration or interpretation.

### What do machines that never break down teach?

This verse invites a thinking person to reflect on the made things around him. Experts build machines of every kind. Some have design faults from the start. Others do not, but machines are machines, however strong the material and flawless the design. Their parts wear, and they need adjustment, repairs and servicing. They stand idle until fixed, sometimes for weeks or months.

Now look at the machines Allah has made. The efficiency and perfection with which they began working on the first day are still there. They run wonderfully without stopping. Their motion is as precise as ever, not a second fast or slow. Their parts never wear out, and they never need a workshop. The reason is that they work "subjected by His command". They need no fuel to drive them and no engine to run them. They work under Allah's command alone, subject to nothing else, so even the slightest breakdown in them is impossible. Yet when the Absolute Master decides to end them, at a time He has fixed, this whole system will fall apart. That day will be the Day of Qiyāmah.

### What do "creation" and "command" mean to the Sufis?

In Sufi thought khalq and amr are two realms. Khalq concerns matter, and amr the subtle realm beyond matter. The verse about the spirit points in this direction. "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the spirit" (17:85), and the answer ties the rūḥ, the spirit, to the command (amr) of the Lord. In this light, "the creation and the command belong to Him" means two things. Everything between the heavens and the earth is made of matter, and its making is called khalq. What lies beyond them, free of matter, has its making called amr.

### What is a human being's place in this order?

Allah is the Creator of the earth, the sky and everything else. He could have created things haphazardly and left them in confusion, but He did not. He linked everything into a perfect, well-ordered and wisely governed system. He set it working so that each thing works exactly as it should to serve the common good.

The human being is a small part of this world. What should his role be in so well-formed a setting? It should be the same as that of everything else. He should give himself to the Creator's plan, as the whole universe has surrendered to it in full obedience. Everything in the universe plays its part in Allah's plan with the utmost excellence (iḥsān), and a person should give himself to it with the same excellence. Nothing in the universe oversteps its set limits, so a person too must not overstep the limits of justice and truth that Allah has laid down.

A human being also has speech and awareness, so his surrender to his Lord must show at that level as well. Knowing and recognising Allah should be so deeply rooted in him that it comes out again and again. He should call on Allah as a subject calls on his Creator and Lord. He should be so aware of Allah's lordship that nothing but Allah stays at the centre of his hopes and fears. He should fear Allah alone and pin his hopes on Him alone. Tying one's fears and hopes to Allah is the highest stage of obedience to Him.

### The inner reading: "Lord" and "Allah", vision and love

The name "Lord" is light itself, and His message is light bound together with love. He is the nurturer of the world's people, the keeper of creatures, the One who repays, the Loving. He is pure and without equal, the judge of every how and why, untouched by anything unworthy. He is evident to Himself in rightness and in being, and evident to the heart in friendship. He is One and sufficient, providing for what everyone has, able to keep hearts upright. He is Lord of everything, keeper of every being, and nurturer of everything able to rise higher.

First He says "Lord", the share of ordinary people. Then He says "Allah", the share of the knowers and the sincerely truthful. "Lord" puts the hearts of good people at ease, and "Allah" carries off the spirits of the knowers. "Lord" gives blessings to those who ask, and "Allah" casts love into the hearts of His friends. "Lord" pours the blessing of vision on the faithful, and "Allah" lights the lamp of love in the knowers through vision.

The master of the spiritual path (ṭarīqah) told of a meeting between Love and Vision. Love compared Vision to light, since it brightens the world. Vision compared Love to fire, since it burns the world. Vision said that whenever it appears, it pulls suffering out of the heart. Love answered that whenever it takes up residence in a heart, it ransacks it. Vision called itself a gift for those who are tried, and Love said that it throws the whole world into uproar.

Vision is the share of those who come to know Him through His works. Their road to Him runs through created, measured and newly arisen things, such as the earth and sky, and the sun, moon and stars held to their courses. Love is the share of those who know Him through Himself. They come from Him to His works, not from His works to Him. The master of the spiritual path said: "Poor is the one who knows Him only through His works! Wretched is the one who loves Him for the sake of His blessings! Foolish is the one who seeks Him by his own effort! Whoever knows Him only through His works worships Him in fear and need."

### In short

- Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, two for the earth, two for its provisions and two for the seven heavens, ending on Friday.
- He could have created all in an instant. The six days teach people to act with care, for haste is from Shayṭān.
- "Established Himself on the Throne" is affirmed as it came, without likening, distorting, denying or asking how, as the Salaf and Imam Mālik taught.
- Night and day, sun, moon and stars run without fault because they are subject to His command alone, until He ends them on the Day of Qiyāmah.
- Creation and command belong to Him alone. A human being should take his place in this order with excellence, keeping Allah's limits and hoping in and fearing Him alone.

55.text:
The previous verse displayed Allah's perfect power and His great blessings. It follows that He alone should be called on, in distress and in need alike: "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Surely He does not like the transgressors". He is the Master of all power, the giver of every blessing and the Lord of all the worlds. To pass Him by and turn elsewhere is ignorance and failure. Allah commands His servants to call on Him, because that secures their good in this life and the next. The verse also sets out rules of manners for supplication, and keeping them raises the hope that a prayer will be answered.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Call upon your Lord"**: in Arabic, duʿāʾ means calling on someone to remove a need. It is also used for remembrance in general. Both senses fit here. In the first, the verse means: ask Allah alone for what you need. In the second it means: make your remembrance (dhikr) and worship for Him alone. Both explanations are reported from early authorities on tafsīr. One explanation addresses the verse to all mankind. Another addresses it to the believers: call on your Lord sincerely, without showing off and without joining anyone with Allah in your prayers.

**"humbly"**: the word is taḍarruʿ. It means feeling one's own helplessness, humility and submission, with a refined lowering of the self. Ibn Jarīr explained it as obeying Him in humility and lowliness. Grammatically it describes the state of the one praying: call on Him in submission. One explanation pairs it with "openly". Another reads the pair as "humbly and out of fear".

**"and secretly"**: the word is khufyah, meaning in private, quietly, with a lowered voice. Ibn Jarīr said it means with humility in your hearts and certainty of His Oneness and lordship, not calling out loudly to show off. A later verse of this surah says the same: "Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence" (7:205).

**"Surely He does not like the transgressors"**: the word al-muʿtadīn comes from iʿtidāʾ, crossing the limits. Allah does not like those who overstep limits, as the translation says. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying this applies in supplication and in other matters too. Abū Mijlaz gave as an example asking to reach the rank of the prophets. Other explanations name those who pray for what is not permitted to them against the righteous, and the boastful and loud-mouthed in their prayers. One of the worst ways to overstep is to call on others besides Him, as the idolaters do.

### Why must supplication be humble?

The first word lays down the first rule. For a prayer to be answered, a person should come before Allah weak, helpless and unable to stand on his own, modest and humble. He should lay aside every trace of pride, dignity, ego and self-regard, and then ask. Supplication is a matter of the soul. Its words should match the weakness and lowliness of the one who asks. Its manner should mirror modesty, and that humility should show even in his outward bearing.

By this standard, much of what passes for supplication today is not supplication at all. It is a reading. Very often people do not know what they are saying, and it has become a routine, as can be seen in many mosques. At the end of the prayer the imam recites some memorised Arabic words of supplication. In some places the imams themselves do not know what the words mean. Even when they do, the less learned in the congregation have no idea. They keep saying "Āmīn, Āmīn" mechanically after the imam without any clue what is being asked. The result of all this performance is the sounding of some words. Supplication has a reality of its own, and here that reality is missing.

It is another matter that Allah, in His boundless mercy, may accept even these lifeless words and give them the effect of answered prayers. Still, everyone should understand that supplication is not read, it is asked. So it matters greatly to ask properly, as one should. And even someone who knows and understands the words of his prayer reduces it to a bland claim if he asks without the right attitude and bearing. No created servant has any right to make such a claim on Allah.

### Why should it be quiet?

The second word teaches that one should ask secretly and in a low voice. That is more meritorious and more likely to be answered. Praying aloud carries three risks. First, it is hard to keep modesty and humility. Second, hypocrisy and the wish for recognition can creep in. Third, the very manner suggests that the one praying hardly knows Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing. He knows what we show and what we hide, and He hears every word, spoken softly or loudly.

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that people once raised their voices in supplication. One account places this during the expedition to Khaybar. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them to go easy on themselves, for they were not calling on someone deaf or absent. The One they were calling, he said, is All-Hearing and Near. Allah Himself describes a righteous man's prayer in the words "when he cried out to his Lord privately" (19:3). This shows that the supplication Allah loves is made in a low, subdued voice.

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said there is a difference of seventy degrees between a supplication made openly and aloud and one made in a low voice. The early righteous elders, he said, strove to the utmost in remembrance and supplication and spent most of their time in it, yet no one heard their voices. Their supplications stayed between them and their Lord. Many had memorised the whole Qur'an and kept reciting it, and others never knew. Some were busy with advanced study of religion and never told anyone. Others came out of their houses after long hours of prayer, and no one learnt of it. He said he had seen people who never did in public any worship they could do in private, and whose voices in supplication were very low.

Ibn Jurayj said that raising the voice and making a noise in supplication is makrūh, disliked. Imam Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ said in his Aḥkām al-Qurʾān that this verse shows a low-voiced supplication to be more meritorious than a loud one. The same is reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Ibn ʿAbbās. He added that the verse also shows that "Āmīn" after Sūrat al-Fātiḥah is better said quietly, because Āmīn, "so be it", is itself a supplication.

### What about the loud prayer after congregational ṣalāh?

In many mosques today, the imams appear to have lost sight of what the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the early elders taught on this point. The supplication after each prayer has become an artificial ritual. Words are recited loudly, which goes against the manners of supplication. It also disturbs the prayer of latecomers who are still completing the part they missed after the imam has finished. The weight of custom has made people blind to these drawbacks.

On a particular occasion, when the aim is for a whole group to make a particular supplication, one person may say the words in a reasonably audible voice while the others say Āmīn. There is no harm in that. The conditions are that it does not disturb anyone else's prayer or worship, and that it does not become a fixed custom. Otherwise ordinary people come to think of it as the standard way of supplicating, as so often happens now.

### Is remembrance better quiet or aloud?

All of the above concerns supplication for one's needs. If duʿāʾ here is taken to mean remembrance and worship, the settled view of the early scholars is that quiet remembrance is better than loud. Shaykhs of the Chishtī order recommend loud remembrance for beginners. They do so as a remedy suited to the seeker's spiritual state, so that voicing it may drive away heedlessness and tune the heart to the remembrance of Allah. Otherwise raising the voice in remembrance is not desirable in itself, even for them. It is permissible, and hadiths support it, on condition that there is no hypocrisy or showing off (riyāʾ) in it.

Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Baihaqī and others report from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ that the Prophet ﷺ said the best remembrance is the hidden kind, and the best provision is what is enough.

Yet at certain times and in certain conditions, voiced remembrance is more desirable and meritorious. The Prophet ﷺ explained these by word and deed. Examples are the adhān and iqāmah, reciting the Qur'an aloud in the prayers that are recited aloud, the takbīrs of prayer and the takbīrs of tashrīq, and the talbiyah in Hajj. So all the Muslim jurists agree that voices must be raised wherever the Prophet ﷺ taught by word or deed to raise them. Everywhere else, silent remembrance is the most preferable and beneficial.

### What counts as overstepping in supplication?

Overstepping, in supplication or anything else, has the same result: Allah does not like it. Looked at closely, the religion of Islam is itself the keeping of limits and the choice to submit and obey. Ṣalāh, ṣawm, Hajj, zakāh and all dealings and transactions stop being worship and become sin once the limits set by the Sharīʿah are crossed in them.

Overstepping in supplication can take several forms.

- Using rhyme and other stylistic flourishes that spoil the humility and submission at its heart.
- Adding needless details. Imam Aḥmad reported, through Abū Niʿāmah, that ʿAbdullāh ibn Mughaffal heard his son ask Allah for the white palace on the right side of Paradise once he entered it. He told his son to ask Allah simply for Paradise and to seek refuge with Him from the Fire. He had heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that people would come who overstep in supplication and in purification. Ibn Mājah and Abū Dāwūd also recorded this hadith, with a good chain that has no fault, and Allah knows best.
- Praying for harm to Muslims in general, or asking Allah for something harmful to them.
- Raising the voice in supplication without need.

### The inner reading: the sinner's sobs

Al-Muṣṭafā said, "Supplication is worship." Supplication is either calling or asking. As calling, it is praise. As asking, it suits the servant. Both are worship and a means of salvation. Yaḥyā Muʿādh said, "Worship of Allah is a storehouse. Its key is supplication, and the teeth of the key are lawful mouthfuls." The condition of supplication is pleading, weeping, and throwing oneself down in lowliness at the Exalted Threshold. That is why He says "humbly and secretly".

A report says that Ādam mourned and pleaded over his slip for a hundred years. At last Jibrīl (Gabriel) said, "Lord, You see Ādam's pleading Yourself, and You hear his weeping. Is there no way for You to accept his apology and put balm on his wound?" The command came: "Jibrīl, leave Ādam to Me. Had I not known this pleading and weeping in him, I would not have decreed the slip for him. I decreed it because I knew that when he became helpless he would loosen his tongue in supplication and pleading. I love My servant to lament and weep before Me. The sobbing of sinners is dearer to Me than the murmuring of those who glorify Me."

A verse like this one is "Call upon Me, I will respond to you" (40:60). It is as if He says: call on Me so that I may answer you, know Me so that I may forgive you, ask of Me so that I may give to you. Elsewhere He speaks of the One "Who responds to the distressed when they cry to Him" (27:62). It is as if He asks: when that poor, helpless man can bear his trial no longer, who but Me will answer him? Who else will hear his plea and come to his aid?

The distressed person has nothing left to hold on to. He looks at his days and sees them scattered to the wind. He sees his hands empty of every means of approach and every act of obedience. His supplication flies like an arrow straight to the target. And one of the conditions of supplication is that one's food be lawful.

### In short

- Since Allah alone has power and gives every blessing, He alone should be called on, for needs and in worship.
- Supplication should be humble, a real asking with understanding, not a mechanical reading of words.
- It is better made quietly, which guards humility and sincerity. Loud remembrance is for occasions the Prophet ﷺ taught, such as the adhān and talbiyah.
- Overstepping in supplication includes artful rhyme, needless details, praying for harm and needless loudness, and Allah does not like those who overstep.

56.text:
The next command joins the manners of supplication to a warning: "Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope and fear. Indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers". Causing corruption after things have been put right does the greatest harm, so Allah forbids it. Instead He commands worship of Him, supplication to Him, earnest asking and humility before Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not spread corruption in the land"**: two opposites meet here, ṣalāḥ and fasād. Ṣalāḥ is the state of being good, right, sound and in order. Fasād is the state of evil, corruption and disorder. Imam Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says in his Mufradāt al-Qurʾān that fasād means something going beyond the bounds of moderation, slightly or greatly. Every corruption grows or shrinks with how far those bounds are crossed, and the further they are crossed, the greater the corruption. Fasād is making things bad, and iṣlāḥ is putting them right. Others explain the corruption as sins and calling people to other than Allah, or as idolatry and acts of disobedience.

**"after it has been set in order"**: after Allah made the earth sound and good, through obedience and the call to Allah. He set it right by sending messengers to it and by establishing things according to His laws. When affairs are in good order and corruption then breaks out, it does the greatest harm to people.

Rāghib also says Allah puts things right in several ways. First, He creates them sound from the start, as in "and improve their condition" (47:2). Second, He removes corruption that has crept into something, as in "He will bless your deeds for you" (33:71). Third, He commands that things be kept in order, and this verse is such a command.

**"And call upon Him with hope and fear."** Worship Him and call on Him, fearing His severe punishment and hoping for His immense reward. Hope that you will enter His Paradise. Call on Allah alone. The manner meant is to fear that the prayer may go unanswered, while placing full hope in His mercy.

**"Indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers"**: Those who receive it are the ones who carry out His commands and keep away from His prohibitions, believers whose words and deeds are good. So be one of them. One explanation takes "mercy" here as Allah's Paradise. In the Arabic, "close" (qarīb) is masculine though "mercy" (raḥmah) is feminine, because mercy is joined to the name of Allah. Another verse says, "But My mercy encompasses everything. I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil" (7:156), that is, for those who have taqwā. Maṭar al-Warrāq said, "Earn Allah's promise by obeying Him, for He has decreed that His mercy is close to the good-doers." Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected this saying.

### What order is meant: outward or inward?

The setting in order of the earth can be taken two ways. The first is outward. Allah made the earth fit to farm and to grow trees. He sent rain from the clouds, so that plants and trees bring forth flowers and fruit, and He made the earth the support of life for humans and animals. The second is inward and spiritual. Allah set the earth right by sending His messengers, His Books and His guidance, cleansing it of kufr, shirk and error. Very possibly the verse means both. Allah has put the earth in order in body and spirit, so do not wreck it with sin and disobedience.

Consider the outward order first. Allah made the earth neither liquid like water, which would be hard to settle on, nor hard like rock or iron, which could not be dug. He made it in between, so that people could soften and level it and make it bear crops, trees, flowers and fruit. They could dig wells, cut moats and canals, and lay firm foundations for houses. Within it and upon it He placed what makes it habitable and lets plants, flowers and fruit grow. From outside it He sent wind, light, heat and cold, and rain from the clouds so that trees could grow. He put the stars and planets to work, sending warm and cool rays that fill flowers and fruit with colour and juice. He gave human beings the intelligence to draw raw materials from the earth, iron and copper, wood and many other metals and stones, and shape them into a new world of industry and craft. That is the outward order, brought about by Allah's perfect power.

The inward, spiritual order rests on remembrance of Allah (dhikr), a living bond with Him, and obedience (iṭāʿah). For this, Allah has placed in every human heart a basic urge to remember and obey Him: "then with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it" (91:8). Around human beings there is not a particle in which He has not placed wonders of His power and astonishing creativity. Seeing them, even a person of ordinary understanding is moved to say, "So Blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators" (23:14). Beyond these signs, He sent His messengers and revealed His Books, which fully established the bond between Creator and creature. So the command is that, now the earth has been set in order outwardly and inwardly, human misdeeds must not ruin it.

### How do sins cause disorder in the physical world?

Just as order has an outward and an inward side, so does disorder, and this verse forbids both. The Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ insist above all on spiritual order, which shuts the door on spiritual disorder. But in this world the two are so linked that disorder in one breeds disorder in the other. So the Sharīʿah of the Qur'an, having closed the doors of spiritual disorder, has also forbidden physical disorder. Theft, robbery, murder and every kind of shamelessness and indecency spread both kinds of disorder. Hence stern restrictions and punishments were laid down for these evils in particular, and ordinary sins were forbidden too. Every sin causes physical disorder at one time and spiritual disorder at another.

That outward disorder leads to inward disorder is obvious. It goes against the command to obey Allah, and disobedience to Allah is simply another name for spiritual disorder. How inward disorder turns into outward disorder takes a little serious thought to see. The whole world and everything in it, great and small, was made by the Master of creation and is subject to His command. As long as human beings obey Allah, everything is harnessed to serve them as it should. When they start disobeying Allah, everything in the world starts disobeying them, from behind a curtain that mortal eyes cannot see through. Careful thought about the effects and outcomes of things gives clear proof of this hostility.

On the surface, people go on using things as normal. Water still quenches thirst, food still removes hunger, and clothes and homes still keep out heat and cold. But judged by their final purpose, none of these things is doing its real job. Their true function is to give peace and comfort, to remove anxiety and to cure illness.

Look at the state of the world today. Comforts and cures have multiplied far beyond anyone's expectations, yet most people suffer severe distress and disease. Diseases no one had heard of appear, and fresh calamities arrive one after another. No one, not even the highest, is content and at peace in his station. In fact, the more these conveniences and products of skill increase, the more disease, anxiety, disaster and hardship increase alongside them. An Urdu saying puts it: the more they treat you, the sicker they make you.

Modern man is spellbound by power and its material gains. If he rose a little above his infatuation with things and technology, he would see that all his inventions, and the society built on them, have failed to give the peace and comfort that were their real purpose. The only reason is the inward disorder described above. We have begun to disobey our Lord, our Creator and Master, and so His creation has begun to disobey us inwardly. It refuses to give us real peace and comfort, however frantically we strive. The famous Maulānā Rūm pointed to this. Earth, air, water and fire, he said, look lifeless and senseless, yet they have a kind of awareness by which they work under their Master's command.

In sum, sin, heedlessness of Allah and disobedience to Him do not only cause spiritual disorder. They lead inevitably to physical disorder as well. The same Maulānā Rūmī says that when people stop paying zakāh the clouds stop bringing rain, and that adultery brings an epidemic that spreads in every direction. This is not poetic fancy. It is a reality firmly supported by the Qur'an and Hadith. And what appears in this world, as disease, epidemics, storms, hurricanes and floods, is only a light foretaste of the final punishment.

So the verse's ban on corruption in the land covers the crimes that disorder the world outwardly. It also covers sin, disobedience and heedlessness of Allah. That is why it goes straight on to say, "call upon Him with hope and fear".

### Why both hope and fear?

Fear and hope together are the two wings of the human soul on its journey of truth and steadfastness. On them it flies high, and by them it reaches the ranks meant for it. As the wording shows, the two should be equal.

Some scholars said that while alive and well, it is fitting to let fear prevail, so that there is no slackness in obedience. When death comes, it is better to let hope prevail. By then the strength to do what should have been done is gone, and nothing remains but to hope for Allah's mercy. This view is recorded in Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ.

Some careful scholars said the real aim is to hold to the straight path of religion and stay constant in obedience to Allah. People's temperaments and tastes differ. Some reach that steadfastness by letting fear lead. Others reach it by letting love and hope lead. Whichever of the two helps a person reach the goal, he should take that route.

### What are the manners of supplication, in sum?

The previous verse gave two rules for supplication, humility and quietness. Both concern the outward person. Taḍarruʿ means that while supplicating one should take on the look and bearing of someone weak, helpless and needy, never proud, arrogant or seemingly self-sufficient. Quietness concerns the mouth and tongue.

This verse gives two inner rules, which concern the heart. The one supplicating should feel in his heart the danger that his prayer may not be answered. At the same time he should hope that it will be. Growing careless about one's faults and sins is contrary to īmān, faith. Losing hope in Allah's boundless mercy is kufr, disbelief. Both are forbidden extremes. Hope of an answer is only rightly held by someone who stays between fear and hope.

### Why does the verse end with mercy?

The closing words, "Allah's mercy is always close to the good-doers", hint that of the two states, hope weighs more. The prayer is made to the Lord of all the worlds. The reach of His mercy cannot be imagined, and His generosity knows no shortage or reluctance. He can answer the prayer of the worst offender, even the prayer of Shayṭān himself. If there is any danger of a prayer going unanswered, it can only come from one's own misdeeds or the weight of one's sins. Being good in deeds is what brings a person close to Allah's mercy.

That is why the Prophet ﷺ spoke of a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, and raises his hands to Allah in supplication. But his food is ḥarām, his drink is ḥarām and his clothing is ḥarām. How, he asked, can such a man's prayer be answered? Muslim and at-Tirmidhī recorded this from Abū Hurairah.

In another hadith, recorded by Muslim and at-Tirmidhī, the Prophet ﷺ said a servant's prayer keeps being answered as long as he does not pray for a sin or for cutting family ties, and does not grow impatient. A Companion asked what growing impatient meant. He explained it as a person thinking he has prayed for so long without an answer, until he loses heart and gives up praying.

In yet another hadith the Prophet ﷺ said that whenever you call on Allah, do so with no doubt that you will be answered. That means keeping one's eyes on Allah's vast mercy and letting the heart trust that the prayer will be answered. This does not conflict with the fear that one's sins may stand in the way.

### Who comes close to Allah's mercy?

The greatest thing a person can achieve is to win Allah's mercy. But Allah's grace falls to the lot of those who bind themselves to Him so fully that all their feelings, without exception, are turned toward Him. They call on Him alone and humble themselves before Him alone. They hope to receive from Him, and they fear Him alone, lest what they have be taken away. People like this seek closeness to Allah, and Allah gives them a place near Him.

### The inner reading: worship as though you see Him

Al-Muṣṭafā said that excellence (iḥsān) is to worship Allah as though you see Him, for even if you do not see Him, He certainly sees you. This report points to the heart meeting the Real, the inmost self drawing near the Unseen, and the spirit beholding Allah. The verse urges the servant to purify his deeds, cut short his worldly hopes, and stay loyal to what he accepted on the day of the covenant, when he said, "Yes indeed" (7:172). Knowing that He watches you, fix your heart on Him and withdraw it from all else. Purify your deeds and be truthful in your states.

The master of the spiritual path (ṭarīqah) said: "Once an eye has seen Him, how can it busy itself with looking at anything else? Once a spirit has found His company, how long will it settle for water and clay? Once someone is used to the presence of contemplation, how can he bear the humiliation of the veil? Would a man who rules his own city choose to live out his days in exile?" "As though you see Him" hints that the Real is to be seen, and "He sees you" is the Real's own seeing.

He also said that once the awe of seeing the Real takes hold, the blame of deniers holds no terror. Serve in a way worthy of the One you worship, he said, not for a share of water and clay, for the awe of beholding the Real is a flood and the approval of people is mere debris.

### In short

- Do not corrupt the earth after Allah has set it in order, outwardly by its design and inwardly by His messengers and Books.
- Sin breeds disorder in the physical world as well as the spiritual, which is why comforts multiply while peace declines.
- Call on Allah with fear and hope together, the two wings of the soul. Carelessness about sin and despair of mercy are both forbidden.
- Hope weighs more, since Allah's mercy is vast and close to those who do good. Unlawful earnings and impatience can block a prayer.
- The highest goodness is to worship Allah as though seeing Him, knowing that He always sees you.

57.text:
Allah has shown that He created the heavens and the earth, owns every affair and makes things serve humankind. He has told people to call on Him in duʿāʾ, since He has power over all things. Now He shows that He is also the Provider, and the One who will raise the dead on the Day of Resurrection: "He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit. Similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful". The previous verses spoke of blessings from above: the heavens, day and night, sun, moon and stars. This verse turns to blessings below, on which the life of humans and of all earthly creatures depends: rain, trees, fields and crops. So Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ explains it. Since no one but Allah meets these needs, people should pray to Him alone for everything and see turning to Him as the key to success.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who sends the winds"**: ar-riyāḥ is the plural of rīḥ, wind. He sends the winds that spread the rain-laden clouds. Another verse says, "And one of His signs is that He sends the winds, ushering in good news ˹of rain˺" (30:46).

**"ushering in His mercy."** The word bushran means good news, and "mercy" here is the rain. Allah Himself sends the winds to announce the coming rain of mercy. There are several readings: nushuran, "spreading out", also read nushran and nashran, and bushran, "bearing good tidings". The singular of the first is nashūr, on the pattern of rasūl, and of the last bashīr. Another verse says, "He is the One Who sends down rain after people have given up hope, spreading out His mercy. He is the Guardian, the Praiseworthy" (42:28). Here the Guardian is al-Walī and the Praiseworthy al-Ḥamīd. Another says, "See then the impact of Allah’s mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same God˺ can raise the dead" (30:50).

**"When they bear heavy clouds"**: saḥāb means cloud, and thiqāl is the plural of thaqīl, heavy. When the winds lift the clouds heavy with water, those clouds hang low and dark.

**"We drive them to a lifeless land"**: sawq means to drive or urge on toward a chosen destination. Balad means a town or settlement, and mayyit means dead. Here the speaker shifts from "He" to "We". A dead land is a dry land without vegetation. Allah drives the clouds there to bring it back to life. Another verse says, "There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life" (36:33).

**"and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit."** We send down water on that land, and by it bring out fruits and crops of every kind.

**"Similarly, We will bring the dead to life"**: just as We revive the earth with plants, We will bring the dead out of their graves and restore them to life on the Day of Resurrection, after they have crumbled away. Allah often draws this comparison in the Qur'an between reviving dead land and the Day of Resurrection.

**"so perhaps you will be mindful"**: so that you may take heed, reflect on Allah's power and the wonders of His creation, and believe that He can raise the dead.

### Why do the winds come before the rain?

It is Allah's way to send cool winds ahead of the rain. They please people, and they also give warning that rain is coming, long before it arrives. So these winds join two blessings. They are good for people and refreshing for all creatures, and they announce the rain in advance. Human beings are delicate creatures. Rain can keep them from their work, and if they know it is coming they can plan for it. Nor are they and their belongings always sheltered from rain. Early signs let most of them take cover for themselves and their goods.

The heavy clouds seem to travel riding on the wind's shoulders. Thousands of tons of water drift along, carried lightly by the wind. What a marvel of divine design, needing no machines and making no human slave over it. It is simplicity itself. When Allah wills, vapour rises from the waters and becomes clouds. Then a sky-filling aircraft, carrying hundreds of thousands of gallons of water in its hold, flies on a cushion of wind to greater heights.

### Why does it say a dead town?

The word balad, a town or settlement, is used here rather than open land. A dead town is a settlement left desolate by lack of water. This suits the real purpose of the rain, which is to water thirsty land so that it grows what people need. The place for that is a settled area, not an uninhabited wilderness where growth is less likely to serve that first purpose.

### Who directs the clouds?

The verse shows, first, that rain comes through the clouds, as everyone can see. So in verses that speak of rain coming down from the sky (samāʾ), the word refers to the clouds. It is also not impossible that some clouds come directly from the sky, rather than rising from the waters like monsoons.

Second, the direction a cloud takes, and the land it goes to, depend directly on Allah's command. He decides the time, the place and the amount of the rain, and the clouds carry out His command. This can be seen everywhere. Sometimes heavy clouds hang over a town in desperate need of rain, and not a drop falls. The clouds move on to the town whose share of water Allah has fixed, and rain falls only there. No one has the power or the boldness to take water from those clouds anywhere else.

Weather scientists have worked out rules for the movement of monsoons. With them they predict where a monsoon rising from the sea will go, and where and how much it will rain. Many countries have weather bureaus for this. Yet experience shows that their forecasts often turn out wrong. When Allah's command runs the other way, their rules fail. Winds and rain clouds turn elsewhere, against the forecast, and the experts can do little about it. Nor do any of their rules contradict the fact that the clouds obey Allah's command. Allah's usual way in this world is for His command to work from behind the curtain of physical causes. Human beings notice those causes and build rules from them, but the reality lies elsewhere.

### How will the dead be raised?

When the dead are raised, Allah will send down rain from the sky, and it will pour on the earth for forty days. The bodies will then grow in their graves as seeds grow in the ground after rain.

Abū Hurairah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said the Horn (ṣūr) will be blown twice on the Day of Qiyāmah. At the first blowing the whole world will perish, and nothing will remain alive. At the second a new world will come into being, and the dead will come to life. There will be forty years between the two blasts, and rain will fall all through them. In that time the scattered parts of every dead human and animal will be gathered, until each has a complete frame. Then, at the second blowing, the rūḥ, the soul, will enter these bodies and they will rise alive. Most of this narration is in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Some parts come from the Kitāb al-Baʿth of Ibn Abī Dāwūd.

So the first verse draws a clear conclusion. The One who brings dead land back to life will have no difficulty bringing back to life human beings who once lived and then died.

### The inner reading: ships to the shore

When hearts breathe in the breeze of nearness, they are carried away into the realm of majesty and stripped of everything outlined and habitual. When the breeze from before time blows from the side of nearness, and the wind of generosity blows from His oneness, servitude turns into freedom and every suffering turns into joy. The fearful reach the shore of safety in the ship of fear. The hopeful reach the shore of His giving in the ship of need. The disobedient reach the shore of repentance in the ship of regret. The one who speaks tawḥīd, Allah's oneness, reaches the shore of being alone with Him in the ship of tawḥīd.

Rain comes from the sky, and the dead earth comes to life with plants, flowers and blossoms. In the same way the rain of mercy comes from the storehouse of His power, and withered hearts come to life. In one heart the seed of regret was planted and watered with success, and he became a renunciant. In another the seed of His care was planted and watered with His kindness, and he became a penitent. In another the seed of awe was planted and watered with reverence, and he became one who knows Allah.

The master of the spiritual path (ṭarīqah) said, "O King, the water of Your care reached a stone, and the stone conceived. Fruit grew from the stone, and the fruit ripened into food. O King, Your remembrance brought the heart to life and cast into it the seed of love. It grew the tree of happiness, and the tree bore the fruit of freedom." Where the ground is soft, the soil sweet and the clay ready to receive, the seed can only become "a good tree" (14:24). It yields nothing but the jasmine of the Covenant.

### In short

- Allah sends winds as heralds of rain, drives the heavy clouds to dead land and brings forth every kind of fruit.
- The winds are a double blessing, refreshing in themselves and a warning that lets people prepare for rain.
- Clouds go where Allah commands. Weather rules describe the causes He works through, but the decision is His.
- Reviving dead land is a picture of the Resurrection, when rain will fall for forty years and the dead will rise at the second blast of the Horn.

58.text:
The rain falls on all land alike, but not all land responds in the same way: "The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord, whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything. This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful". When rain comes it falls on rivers and mountains, on good land and bad. Yet plants grow only where the land is able to grow them. Rocky and sandy ground gains nothing from the rain.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The fertile land"**: good land with rich soil, and one explanation adds land that is not a swamp.

**"produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord"**: its plants come up quickly and well, with Allah's permission, without toil or strain. A similar expression is used of Maryam (Mary), mother of ʿĪsā (Jesus): "blessed her with a pleasant upbringing" (3:37). One explanation compares the good land to the sincere believer, who does what Allah commands willingly and gladly. Another compares it to the believer who heeds a reminder when he hears it, benefits from it and acts rightly.

**"whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything."** The word nakid means something both worthless and scanty. On hard, barren, salty or swampy land, little grows at all, and only with toil and great difficulty. Whatever does grow is small in quantity and poor in quality. Mujāhid and others, among them as-Sibākh, said the same. One explanation compares this land to the hypocrite, who does what Allah commands only when forced and without any goodwill. Another compares it to the disbeliever, who gains nothing from the true teachings he receives and does no deed that benefits him.

**"This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful"**: in this way Allah sets out His signs and proofs in different forms, explaining the Qur'an through the parable of the believer and the disbeliever. He does it to confirm the truth for people who are thankful for His blessings, who believe and follow their Lord. The message was for everyone. Yet in the end it benefited only those who had the capacity for it and recognised its true worth.

### What is the parable of the rain?

Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Mūsā that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ compared the guidance and knowledge Allah sent him with to abundant rain falling on land of three kinds.

1. One part was fertile. It soaked up the water and grew grass and plants in plenty.
2. Another part was hard ground that held the water. Allah let people benefit from it: they drank from it, watered their animals and irrigated their crops.
3. A third part was barren. It neither held the water nor grew anything.

The first is like the person who understands Allah's religion and benefits from what the Prophet ﷺ brought, learning it and teaching it to others. The last is like the person who pays it no attention and does not accept the guidance he was sent with.

### Why does guidance take root in some hearts and not others?

Allah's guidance, His revealed Books, His blessed prophets, and the teaching and training of their heirs, the scholars and spiritual guides, are like the rain. They reach everyone. But just as not every piece of land benefits from the rain, only those able to absorb this spiritual rain benefit from it. Some hearts are like rocky or sandy ground, with no capacity to absorb it and grow. They cling to their errors despite clear guidance, signs and scriptures. The closing words hint at this. Allah's guidance and clear signs are open to all, like the rain, but only the grateful benefit, those who value what they receive.

Allah has made the world so that its material events stand for spiritual truths. When rain falls, the water reaches every part of a place, but different lands use it differently. One area turns into lush green fields. Another, after the same rain, stays as it was and grows nothing but scrub. So it is with the spiritual rain that comes from Allah as His guidance. Its message reaches every ear, but each person benefits according to how receptive he is.

The one who is ready to accept the truth draws its full benefit. He gains a new life from it, and his nature suddenly comes awake. His bond with his Almighty Lord is formed, and his parched soul blossoms with divine inspiration. The one who has lost his natural receptivity is the opposite. For all its rich promise, the rain of guidance does him no good at all, and he stays as dry as before. If anything grows, it is a thin crop of scrub. In him the rain of guidance breeds jealousy, arrogance, hollow sophistry and opposition to the truth, so he fails to accept it and stand by it.

For land to soak up rain, it must be dry. If it is not, the water runs off the surface without sinking in. In the same way, Allah's guidance takes root only in someone who longs for it, who has emptied his soul of the dross of this world. Another person is careless of Allah's guidance, with a heart absorbed in other interests and other glories. He may meet the guidance, but it will not soak into him. It will not feed his soul, water its ground or help the garden of Allah grow there.

### The inner reading: the good heart

One of them said, "Its goodness comes from lasting security, the justice of the ruler and the obedience of the obedient." Abū ʿUthmān said, "This is the heart of the faithful, on whose limbs the lights of obedience appear. 'Whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything' is the heart of the disbeliever, on whose limbs only acts of opposition appear."

### In short

- Rain falls on every land, but only good land yields a rich harvest. Bad land yields little, and with difficulty.
- In the same way, Allah's guidance reaches everyone, but only receptive and grateful hearts benefit from it.
- The Prophet ﷺ likened his guidance to rain falling on fertile, water-holding and barren ground.
- A heart must long for guidance and be emptied of worldly dross for guidance to take root in it.

59.text:
The surah now opens a long series of prophets' stories, beginning with Nūḥ (Noah): "Indeed, We sent Noah to his people. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”" From its start up to this point, the surah has set out the basic principles of Islam: tawḥīd (Allah's oneness), risālah (messengership) and the Hereafter. It has proved them in different ways, urged people to follow them and warned against opposing them, and shown how Shayṭān leads people astray. After Allah told the story of Ādam (Adam) at the beginning, He now tells the stories of the prophets in order, from the first to the later ones.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We sent Noah to his people."** The Arabic word laqad, "indeed", answers an oath that is left unstated. The verse shows that his mission was to his own people alone, not to all mankind. They lived in Iraq. They were outwardly civilised but sunk in shirk, associating partners with Allah. Allah sent him to call them to Allah's oneness and to give up worshipping anything besides Him.

**"He said, “O my people! Worship Allah"**: worship Allah alone and declare His oneness. This first sentence is the call to worship Allah, the heart of the whole principle.

**"you have no other god except Him."** You have no true god but the One I am calling you to. This second sentence urges them to give up shirk and kufr, which had spread among them like an epidemic. In the Arabic, "other" can be read ghayrihi, describing "god", or ghayruhu, standing in its place.

**"I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”"** I fear you will be struck by it if you do not believe and keep worshipping others besides Him. He meant the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, should you come before Allah still joining partners with Him. This third sentence warns of the great punishment they would face if they refused. It could mean the punishment of the Hereafter, and also the punishment of the Flood in this world.

### Why does the series of prophets begin with Nūḥ?

From the eighth section (rukūʿ) almost to the end of the surah comes the account of several prophets and their peoples, about fourteen sections in all. Its subject is the shared principles of tawḥīd, messengership and the Hereafter. Every prophet called his people to these universal principles. He gave good news of reward to those who believed, and warned of punishment and a bitter end for those who refused. Hundreds of basic and secondary rulings come up along the way. Later peoples could learn from the fate of earlier ones. For the Prophet ﷺ it was a comfort to know that the other prophets had met the same treatment.

The first prophet in the chain was Ādam (Adam), but his was not a time of struggle against disbelief and error. Most of the laws given to him concerned settling the earth and managing human needs, and disbelief and disbelievers did not yet exist. The struggle against kufr and shirk began with Nūḥ. In terms of the prophetic mission and a code of law, he was Allah's first rasūl, the first messenger to the inhabitants of the earth after Ādam. Also, after the great Flood drowned the world, the only survivors were Nūḥ and those with him in the Ark, and the new world was peopled through them. That is why he is also called the second Ādam. So he comes first in this account, which tells of his nine hundred and fifty years of struggle against the crooked ways of most of his people. In the end all but a few believers were drowned.

### Who was Nūḥ, and when did he live?

His lineage is given as Nūḥ son of Lamak, son of Matūshalakh, son of Khanūkh. Khanūkh, as they claim, was the prophet Idrīs (Enoch), the first person to write with a pen. Idrīs's own line runs back through Barad, Mahlīl, Qanīn, Yānish and Shīth to Ādam. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq and other experts in genealogy recorded this lineage. Whether Nūḥ came before or after Idrīs is debated. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ reports that most of the Companions held that Nūḥ came before Idrīs.

Nūḥ was in the eighth generation after Ādam. Al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that ten qarn separated Ādam and Nūḥ. Al-Ṭabarānī reports the same from a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ narrated by Abū Dharr. A qarn generally means a hundred years, so by this narration the gap was a thousand years. Ibn Jarīr reported that Nūḥ was born eight hundred and twenty-six years after Ādam's death. The Qur'an states plainly that Nūḥ lived nine hundred and fifty years, and a hadith says Ādam lived nine hundred and sixty. That makes a total of two thousand eight hundred and fifty-six years from Ādam's birth to Nūḥ's death. Some narrations give Nūḥ's real name as Shākir, others as Sakan, and others as ʿAbd al-Ghaffār. Al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak also reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ said Nūḥ was made a prophet at forty and lived sixty years after the Flood.

### How did idol worship begin?
