For about a thousand years after Ādam, his descendants held to the belief in Allah's oneness. Then, as ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and several other scholars of tafsīr explained, some righteous men died. Their people built places of worship over their graves and made images of them, to remember their righteousness and devotion and to copy them. As time passed they made statues of them, and later worshipped those idols, naming them after the righteous men: Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq and Nasr. Gradually these great men took on the status of gods among the people of ancient Iraq. When this evil had spread so far, Allah sent Nūḥ as His messenger to reform them, and all praise is due to Him.

### In short

- After Ādam's story, the surah begins the stories of the prophets with Nūḥ, the first messenger sent to confront shirk and the "second Ādam" through whom the world was repeopled.
- Idol worship began when people made images of righteous men to remember them, and later worshipped them.
- Nūḥ called his people in Iraq to worship Allah alone, to give up shirk, and to fear the punishment of a tremendous Day.
- He lived nine hundred and fifty years. Accounts give about a thousand years between Ādam and Nūḥ.

60.text:
The leading men of his people answered him with scorn: "But the chiefs of his people said, “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”" The word for chiefs, malaʾ, means the headmen, nobles and powerful elders of a community.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But the chiefs of his people said"**: the leaders, notables, commanders and great men of his people, the respected elders of their council, spoke for the rest.

**"“We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”"** We think you are plainly wrong in what you say, O Nūḥ (Noah). They said this because he called them to give up the idols they had found their forefathers worshipping. In effect they told him that he was trying to pull them away from their ancestral faith. They added that his talk of rising on a Last Day to be rewarded or punished was mere superstition.

### Why do the wicked call the righteous misguided?

This is the way of evil people. They see the righteous as the ones who have gone astray. Allah says elsewhere, "And when they saw the faithful, they would say, “These ˹people˺ are truly astray,”" (83:32). He also says:

> "The disbelievers say of the believers, “Had it been ˹something˺ good, they would not have beaten us to it.” Now since they reject its guidance, they will say, “˹This is˺ an ancient fabrication!”" (46:11).

There are other verses on the same theme. Nūḥ's people did not hesitate to call the prophet of their time foolish and misguided. In their eyes he had left the religion of their great forefathers.

### In short

- The chiefs of Nūḥ's people accused him of plain error for calling them away from their ancestors' idols.
- They also dismissed his warnings of resurrection and judgement as superstition.
- Evil people have always seen the righteous as the ones who are astray.

61.text:
Their words were harsh, but Nūḥ (Noah) answered them as a prophet should: "He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds". He did not meet anger with anger. He tried to clear away their doubts in the simplest words, leaving a model for everyone who calls others to the truth, every preacher and reformer.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided!"** Nūḥ told the leaders of his people that there was nothing wrong with him, and no foolishness in him. He was not in error, as they claimed. The Arabic word ḍalālah here is more general than aḍ-ḍalāl, "misguidance". So denying it denies more: not even a trace of error is in him.

**"But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"**: I am rightly guided by my Lord, and I am His messenger to you, the messenger of the Lord and King of all things. He is my Lord, your Lord and the Lord of all creation.

### What does "Lord of all worlds" answer?

Nūḥ was saying that their charge of error was false. Admittedly, he did not follow the customs of their forefathers, which were rooted in ignorance. Instead he had been sent as a messenger from the Lord of all the worlds. That one phrase strikes decisively at shirk. Once its meaning is grasped, no god or goddess of any kind can stand as a rightful object of worship.

### In short

- Nūḥ answered his people's insults calmly, a model for everyone who calls others to the truth.
- He denied even the smallest trace of error, and declared himself a messenger of the Lord of all worlds.
- Calling Allah "Lord of all worlds" leaves no room for any other object of worship.

62.text:
Nūḥ (Noah) goes on to describe his mission, completing the reply that runs across these two verses (7:61-62): "conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know". Everything he told them came under his Lord's guidance. His only task was to deliver Allah's message, which was for their own good. It brought no benefit to Allah and served no interest of his own.

### Phrase by phrase

**"conveying to you my Lord’s messages"**: I deliver only the revelation Allah has sent me with, explaining His commands and prohibitions. The verb can be read ublighukum or uballighukum.

**"and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice."** I want only good for you. I urge you to follow what Allah has commanded and earn its reward. I warn you against what He has forbidden and the punishment for disobeying Him. I call you to repentance and faith.

**"And I know from Allah what you do not know"**: I know, through the revelation Allah has given me, the punishment that awaits you if you do not believe. Your doubts about the punishment of the Last Day come from not knowing, while Allah has given me certainty about it.

### What marks a true messenger?

These are the qualities of a messenger. He conveys the message in plain yet eloquent words, gives sincere advice, and knows Allah. In these no other people can compete with the prophets.

Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that on the Day of ʿArafah, when the gathering was larger than ever, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his Companions what they would say when they were asked about him. They said they would testify that he had conveyed the message, delivered it and given sincere advice. He then kept raising his finger toward the sky and lowering it toward the people, saying, "O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness."

### Why did they object that he was only a man?

Nūḥ's people raised another doubt, recorded in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn. To them he was simply a mortal, eating and drinking, sleeping and waking just as they did. How could they take him as their leader? If Allah had wanted to send them a message, He would have sent angels, whose rank and grandeur would have impressed them. All they saw was a man of their own race and people who wanted to lord it over them:

> "But the disbelieving chiefs of his people said ˹to the masses˺, “This is only a human like you, who wants to be superior to you. Had Allah willed, He could have easily sent down angels ˹instead˺. We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers" (23:24).

The answer to this doubt comes in the next verse.

### In short

- Nūḥ's only task was to deliver Allah's messages and advise his people sincerely, for their good and not his own.
- He knew from revelation what they did not: the punishment awaiting them if they refused to believe.
- Clear delivery, sincere advice and knowledge of Allah are the marks of every messenger. The Prophet ﷺ had his Companions bear witness that he had conveyed the message.
- His people objected that he was only a man and that angels should have been sent.

63.text:
Nūḥ (Noah) answers his people's surprise that a man like them should bring a message: "Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own, warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”" Do not wonder at this. It is nothing odd that Allah should send revelation to a man from among you, out of mercy, kindness and compassion for you.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you find it astonishing"**: indeed you do find it odd, and in effect you deny it.

**"that a reminder should come to you from your Lord"**: the reminder is prophethood, an admonition, revelation and good teaching from your Lord.

**"through one of your own"**: through the tongue of a man from among you, a human being like you. One explanation adds: a man you know well, who grew up among you, who has never been a liar or misguided, and who has not come to you from some other people.

**"warning you"**: so that he may warn you of punishment if you do not believe.

**"so you may beware"**: so that you may fear Allah, obey Him, and avoid His punishment by worshipping none but Him.

**"and perhaps be shown mercy?”"** So that his warning may lead you to stop opposing him, and you may receive mercy through faith and be spared the torment.

### Why must a messenger be human?

The argument is that it is no cause for surprise if a human being is made Allah's messenger. First, Allah is the Absolute Master. Choosing someone for prophethood or messengership is His alone, and He does it as He wills. No one may dare insist otherwise.

Second, a little thought shows that the purpose of sending a messenger to guide human beings can only be served by a human being. It is a task angels cannot perform. The aim of prophethood is to bring people to believe in and obey Allah, and to save them from the bitter results of defying His commands. That is possible only when someone of their own kind sets before them a living model of that conduct. He must show them that one can worship Allah and keep His commands while still meeting ordinary human needs and desires.

Had angels brought the call and set the example, people could easily have said that angels have no human desires. They never feel hunger or thirst, never sleep and never tire, so how could anyone become like them? But when one of their own kind, with all the usual human traits and desires, walks among them as a perfect model of obedience to Allah, they are left with no excuse. The words "warning you, so you may beware" point to this. The one whose warning can make people fear must be of their kind, a full embodiment of human nature like them.

The disbelievers of many peoples have raised this same doubt, questioning whether a human being could be a prophet or messenger. This is the Qur'an's answer to every such doubt. It is sad that despite so many clear statements in the Qur'an, some people go as far as denying the humanity of the Prophet ﷺ.

### Why do people reject a messenger they know?

The ignorant fail to see this truth. They simply refuse to accept that someone of their own kind could stand above them. That is why they nurse hatred for the friends of Allah (awliyāʾ) and the scholars (ʿulamāʾ) of their own time, and look down on them because they are contemporaries. This has always been the mark of the ignorant.

Nūḥ's people were the same. They found it very hard to accept that a man who seemed just like them had been chosen to deliver Allah's message. They compared him with the great men whose religion they claimed to follow, whose greatness was fixed in the records of history. Beside them, Nūḥ, their contemporary with no glory attached to his name, looked like an ordinary man. His goodwill, his strong arguments, his reasoning and his firm stand on the path of truth did not move them. So they refused to accept him, and they would not take up the way of righteousness and fear of Allah (taqwā). All they could say was that their forefathers knew better.

### In short

- Nūḥ told his people there was nothing odd in a reminder coming from their Lord through a man from among them.
- Choosing a messenger is Allah's right alone. Only a human can show by example that obedience is possible alongside human needs.
- An angel's example would leave people an excuse, and a human's leaves them none.
- The ignorant despise the righteous of their own time and revere only great names from the past, as Nūḥ's people did.

64.text:
When Nūḥ's (Noah's) fatherly, well-meaning answers made no impression on his heartless people, Allah sent the punishment of the Flood: "But they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and drowned those who rejected Our signs. They were certainly a blind people". The full story of Nūḥ, the drowning of his people and the rescue of those in the Ark comes in Sūrah Hūd and Sūrah Nūḥ. This verse gives the gist that suits the context here.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But they rejected him"**: they ignored his good counsel completely and did not believe in Allah. They insisted on denying and opposing him, and only a few of them believed, as another verse states. In the end Nūḥ asked Allah to destroy the disbelievers.

**"so We saved him and those with him in the Ark"**: Allah saved Nūḥ and the believers with him from drowning and from the punishment, by letting them take refuge in the Ark (the fulk, the ship).

**"and drowned those who rejected Our signs."** He drowned those who denied His Scripture and His messenger Nūḥ, by means of a great flood, as their punishment. Another verse says, "So because of their sins, they were drowned, then admitted into the Fire. And they found none to help them against Allah" (71:25).

**"They were certainly a blind people"**: blind to the truth, unable to recognise it or find their way to it. Their hearts were blind to guidance, and they disbelieved in Allah.

### When does Allah's punishment come?

Zayd ibn Aslam said that when the Flood overtook Nūḥ's people, they were at the height of their numbers and power. The lands and mountains of Iraq could hardly hold them. It has always been Allah's way to keep giving the disobedient respite. He sends His punishment when they have reached the peak of their numbers, power and wealth, and are drunk, as it were, on their success.

### How many were in the Ark?

Reports differ on how many were in Nūḥ's Ark. According to a report that reached Ibn Wahb, Ibn ʿAbbās put the number rescued with Nūḥ on the ship at eighty men. One of them was called Jurhum, and he spoke Arabic. Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected this, and it is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās with a continuous chain. Some narrations say the eighty were made up of forty men and forty women. After the Flood they settled at a place near Mosul in Iraq, which became known as Thamānūn, "Eighty".

### What does Nūḥ's story teach?

Here Allah tells how He took vengeance on His enemies, saved His messenger and those who believed in him, and destroyed their disbelieving enemies. He says elsewhere, "We certainly help Our messengers and the believers, ˹both˺ in this worldly life and on the Day the witnesses will stand forth" (40:51). This is Allah's way (sunnah) with His servants in this life and the next: the good end, victory and triumph belong to those who fear Him.

The brief account of Nūḥ at this point teaches three things.

1. The call of all the earlier prophets, and their basic articles of faith, were one and the same.
2. Allah supports His chosen messengers in astonishing ways. They were in no danger even when surrounded by a flood rising to the mountain peaks.
3. Denying Allah's noble prophets invites His punishment. The warning still stands. As earlier peoples were punished for denying their prophets, a similar fate could overtake their modern counterparts, so they would do well not to grow careless and unafraid.

### What kind of blindness is meant?

When Nūḥ had fully conveyed the divine message and his people rejected it, they were drowned in the great Flood. The reason was that they had denied and belied Allah's signs. They wanted Allah's message to come through an established, celebrated figure, not an "ordinary man". In Allah's eyes that was blindness. Allah gave human beings insight so that they would recognise the truth in the form of signs, not through some tangible proof. Those who do not recognise the truth in its signs are blind in Allah's eyes, though they have eyes. Such people have no share in Allah's grace.

### In short

- Nūḥ's people persisted in denial, so Allah saved him and the believers in the Ark and drowned the rest.
- Allah gives the disobedient respite and then seizes them at the height of their power and pride.
- About eighty people were saved, among them Jurhum, who spoke Arabic.
- Victory belongs to the messengers and the God-fearing. Those who will not see the truth in Allah's signs are truly blind.

65.text:
As Allah sent Nūḥ (Noah) to his people, so He sent one of their own to the people of ʿĀd: "And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. Will you not then fear Him?”" This is the second story in the series. It tells of the Prophet Hūd and a mighty people whose blessings turned into a curse through their own crooked thinking.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd."** Hūd was their prophet. He is called their brother because Hūd and the people of ʿĀd share a family tree. Both are in the fifth generation after Nūḥ, descended from his son Sām, and their lines meet in Sām. So Hūd was their brother by lineage. One explanation calls them "the earlier ʿĀd".

**"He said, “O my people! Worship Allah"**: worship Allah alone and affirm His oneness.

**"you have no other god except Him."** You have no true god but the One I am calling you to.

**"Will you not then fear Him?”"** Will you not have taqwā, fearing Him and so believing? Will you not guard yourselves against worshipping others besides Him, by following His instructions and avoiding what He has forbidden, so that you are saved from His punishment? The terrible punishment of Nūḥ's people was still fresh in people's minds in Hūd's time. So he had no need to describe how severe Allah's punishment of the disobedient could be. It was enough to ask, "Will you not then fear Him?"

### Who were ʿĀd?

ʿĀd was the name of a man in the fifth generation after Nūḥ, from the line of his son Sām. His descendants and his people came to be known by his name. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said the tribe of ʿĀd descended from ʿĀd, son of Iram, son of ʿAws, son of Sām, son of Nūḥ. These are the ancient ʿĀd whom Allah mentions, the children of ʿĀd son of Iram, who lived in the desert among lofty pillars. Allah says:

> "Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ’Ȃd— ˹the people˺ of Iram—with ˹their˺ great stature, unmatched in any other land" (89:6-8).

That was because of their might and strength. Another verse says:

> "As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, “Who is superior to us in might?” Did they not see that Allah ˹Himself˺, Who created them, was far superior to them in might? Still they persisted in denying Our signs" (41:15).

The Qur'an also speaks of "ʿĀd the First" and of "Iram" (89:7). This shows that the people of ʿĀd are also known by the name Iram, and that besides the first ʿĀd there was a second. Commentators and historians differ on the details. The better-known view is that Iram was ʿĀd's grandfather. This ʿĀd, descended from ʿAws, son of Iram, is called the first ʿĀd. Iram's second son, Jathw, had a son named Thamūd, who is called the second ʿĀd. So ʿĀd and Thamūd are two branches of Iram. Some commentators say that when the punishment struck ʿĀd, a delegation of theirs was visiting Makkah and escaped it, and they are known as the other ʿĀd.

Another account says that Iram, Nūḥ's grandson, was among the believers saved in the Ark, and was the forefather of the tribe of ʿĀd. They settled in Yemen and at first followed the religion of Nūḥ. Later they strayed from the right path, and Allah appointed Hūd as their prophet.

### Where did they live, and what were they like?

The people of ʿĀd lived in Yemen, in the region of al-Aḥqāf, which means sand dunes. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq reported from Abū aṭ-Ṭufayl ʿĀmir ibn Wāthilah that he heard ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib speak to a man from Ḥaḍramawt. ʿAlī asked whether he had seen a red sand dune, with a lot of arāk and lote trees around it, in a certain part of Ḥaḍramawt. The man said yes, and that ʿAlī described it as if he had seen it himself. ʿAlī said he had not seen it, but it had been described to him. When the man asked what was special about it, ʿAlī said that the grave of the Prophet Hūd lay close by. Ibn Jarīr recorded this. It shows that ʿĀd lived in Yemen, since their prophet was buried there.

ʿĀd had thirteen clans, and their settlements stretched from Oman to Ḥaḍramawt and Yemen. Their lands were fertile and full of gardens, and they built mansions and palaces to live in. They were tall and powerfully built, which is what the later phrase about increased stature (7:69) refers to. Allah had opened the doors of His blessings to them. But their crooked thinking turned those very blessings into a curse. They grew so drunk on their power and grandeur that they boasted, "Who is superior to us in might?" (41:15). How odd that they ignored their Lord, the Lord of the worlds, while bathed in His blessings, and sank into worshipping idols carved from rock.

Hūd was one of the noble men and chiefs of ʿĀd, for Allah chooses His messengers from the best and most honourable families and tribes. His people were mighty and strong, but their hearts were just as hard. They were among the nations that most denied the truth. His message to them was the worship of Allah alone with no partner, together with obedience to Him and fear of Him.

### What became of them?

Hūd urged ʿĀd to leave idol worship for pure monotheism, to give up injustice and oppression, and to practise moderation and fairness. Drunk with power and wealth, they would not listen. So the first punishment came: no rain fell for three years in a row. Their lands turned to desert and their gardens to dead wood. Still they clung to kufr, shirk and idol worship. Then came the second punishment, the windstorm described under verse 72, and ʿĀd were wiped out to the last man.

When the punishment came, Hūd and his companions took shelter in an open space fenced with stakes. Remarkably, the wind that brought palaces crashing down on their pillars slowed when it entered this enclosure and blew in gently. Hūd and his companions sat there in peace, untroubled, even while the punishment was falling. After ʿĀd were destroyed, they moved to Makkah and lived there until they died. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ records this.

The Qur'an states plainly and decisively that ʿĀd's punishment came as a windstorm. In Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, after the story of Nūḥ (Noah), Allah says, "Then We raised another generation after them" (23:31). This other generation clearly seems to be ʿĀd. After describing their words and deeds, it says, "Then the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them with justice" (23:41). On the basis of this verse, some commentators say ʿĀd's punishment was aṣ-Ṣaiḥah, a harsh, terrifying blast of sound. There is no contradiction. Both may have happened.

### Where did the Arabic language begin?

The well-known Arab genealogist Abū al-Barakāt al-Jaunī wrote that Hūd's son was Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān, who went to live in Yemen. The people of Yemen descend from him. He said the Arabic language began with him, and that the language was called Arabic, and its speakers Arabs, after the name Yaʿrub. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ records this.

The truth is that Arabic existed from the time of Nūḥ. He had a companion in the Ark named Jurhum, who spoke Arabic, and the settling of Makkah began with this same Jurhum. Still, it is possible that Arabic took shape in Yemen through Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān, and that this is what Abū al-Barakāt meant.

### In short

- Allah sent the Prophet Hūd to ʿĀd, his brother by descent, since both traced their line to Sām son of Nūḥ.
- ʿĀd were a tall, powerful people of Yemen with fertile gardens and grand palaces, who boasted that no one was mightier.
- Hūd called them to worship Allah alone and to fear Him, a short reminder since the Flood was still remembered.
- Drought came first and then the wind, while Hūd and his companions sat safely in an enclosure and later moved to Makkah.
- Hūd's grave is reported to lie in Ḥaḍramawt. Arabic existed from Nūḥ's time, though it may have taken shape in Yemen.

66.text:
The leaders of ʿĀd answered the Prophet Hūd much as Nūḥ's (Noah's) people had answered Nūḥ, with only the words changed: "The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.”" To them he did not seem to have the greatness they expected in a prophet, so they concluded that he was either a fool or making a false claim.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded"**: the leaders and notables of his people who disbelieved in Allah and rejected His messenger. They spoke for the general public, the chiefs, masters and commanders among them.

**"“We surely see you as a fool"**: we think you foolish, ignorant and backward, misguided for calling us to leave the idols and worship Allah alone.

**"and we certainly think you are a liar.”"** In fact, they say, we are sure you are lying in your message when you claim that Allah has sent you.

### Why did the call to one God seem foolish to them?

The leaders of ʿĀd thought the call to give up their many idols for One God was folly. In the same way, the chiefs of Quraysh later marvelled at the call to worship One God:

> "Has he reduced ˹all˺ the gods to One God? Indeed, this is something totally astonishing.”" (38:5).

In their eyes Hūd did not have the stature they thought a prophet should have. So they decided he must be either a fool or a liar.

### In short

- The disbelieving chiefs of ʿĀd called Hūd a fool and a liar for calling them to worship Allah alone.
- Their stance repeated that of Nūḥ's people, and Quraysh would later show the same astonishment at the call to One God.
- They expected a prophet to have outward greatness, and when they did not see it, they dismissed him.

67.text:
The Prophet Hūd answered calmly, much as Nūḥ (Noah) had answered his people (7:61-63): "Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds". He was not what they claimed. He had brought them the truth from Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool!"** There is no folly or ignorance in me, nor am I backward, as you claim.

**"But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"**: I bring you the truth from Allah, who created everything and is the Lord and King of all things. I am His messenger to you.

### What does his calm reply show?

They had insulted him as a fool and a liar, yet he did not answer insult with insult. He simply denied the charge and stated the plain truth of his mission. This is how the prophets answer, and it is the model for everyone who calls others to Allah.

### In short

- Hūd denied any folly and declared himself a messenger of the Lord of all worlds.
- His calm reply mirrors Nūḥ's, and shows the prophetic way of answering abuse with truth rather than anger.

68.text:
The Prophet Hūd describes his task: "conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor". These are the qualities of the prophets: delivering the message, sincerity and trustworthiness.

### Phrase by phrase

**"conveying to you my Lord’s messages."** I deliver only what Allah has told me to deliver to you, explaining His commands and prohibitions. That is, that you should believe in Allah's oneness and His sacred law.

**"And I am your sincere advisor"**: I am a trustworthy adviser to you all. I warn you of Allah's punishment and call you to repentance and faith. I am trustworthy in conveying my Lord's message, delivering what I was told, no less and no more. One explanation adds a point. You used to regard me as trustworthy, so how can you now call me a liar?

### What should a caller to the truth feel toward his hearers?

Literally Hūd says, "I am your well-wisher." This shows that a caller to the truth is not his hearers' rival or competitor. Between them there is goodwill and trust. The caller should hold nothing in his heart for them but good wishes. However rude and unpleasant they are, he should remain their well-wisher to the last moment.

When he delivers his message, he should not feel that he is handing over something of his own. Rather, the message is theirs. He is only its trustee, and in handing it over he frees himself of a heavy responsibility.

### In short

- Hūd's task was to deliver his Lord's messages exactly, as a sincere and trustworthy adviser.
- A caller to the truth is his hearers' well-wisher, never their rival, however they treat him.
- He delivers the message as a trust that belongs to them, not as a favour of his own.

69.text:
The people of ʿĀd raised the same objection as Nūḥ's (Noah's) people: how could they accept a human being like themselves as their superior? Had he been an angel, perhaps they would. The Prophet Hūd answers as Nūḥ did, and then reminds them of Allah's favours: "Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you? Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature. So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord"**: indeed you think it a marvel. The reminder is prophethood.

**"through one of your own"**: through the tongue of a man from among you, a human being like you, not through an angel or a jinn.

**"so he may warn you?"** So that he may warn you of Allah's punishment, His "Days" of torment, and of the meeting with Him. Do not be surprised that Allah has sent you a messenger from among yourselves to warn you. Rather than wonder at it, thank Allah for this blessing. There is nothing odd in a human being coming as Allah's messenger to put His fear into people's hearts. It is a human being who can convince other human beings.

**"Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah"**: He established you on the earth as successors after the people of Nūḥ, who were destroyed for their disbelief. Remember His favour in making you descendants of Nūḥ. It was at Nūḥ's supplication that the people of the earth were destroyed, once they had defied and opposed him. So thank Allah and praise Him.

**"and increased you greatly in stature."** He made you taller than other people and gave you greater height, bulk and strength. One explanation says the tallest of them measured 100 feet and the shortest 60. Allah says something similar of Ṭālūt (Saul): "blessed him with knowledge and stature" (2:247).

**"So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful.”"** Remember His blessings and graces, and believe in Him. Then you may prosper, gain what you hope for, and escape what you fear, Allah's wrath and punishment.

### Why do the prophets speak of blessings?

Remembering these blessings would have been for ʿĀd's own good. But they were wicked and drunk on power and wealth, so they paid no attention.

The prophets' call has always rested on two things. They remind people of the blessings given to them, and they warn that if they are not grateful to Allah they will suffer His punishment. Prophets never make communal or material issues the subject of their preaching. They do their best to keep their exchanges with their hearers on the truths that really matter. They want to be known to their people only as callers to the One God and to the Hereafter. That is all they say.

"Remember Allah's favours, so you may be successful" shows that the blessings of the Hereafter are earned only by someone who has acknowledged Allah's grace in this world. Paradise is the greatest expression of Allah's grace and generosity. So the Paradise of the Hereafter will be reached by the one who has found and recognised Allah's grace and generosity here. That recognition is the real price of Paradise.

### In short

- ʿĀd, like Nūḥ's people, wondered that a human being should bring Allah's message. Hūd told them it was a blessing to be thankful for.
- He reminded them that Allah made them successors to Nūḥ's people and gave them great stature and strength.
- The prophets' call reminds people of Allah's blessings and warns against ingratitude, without turning to worldly issues.
- Recognising Allah's grace in this world is the real price of Paradise.

70.text:
The answer of the people of ʿĀd shows their rebellion, defiance and stubbornness: "They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!”" Their reply was no different from the one people who have gone astray usually give.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone"**: have you come to tell us to worship Allah alone?

**"and abandon what our forefathers used to worship?"** Must we give up the many gods our parents and ancestors worshipped? That, they meant, they would never do. If Hūd hoped to pull them away from their ancestors' faith, so that they would drop their idols and believe in One God, he would not succeed.

**"Then bring us what you threaten us with"**: then let the punishment you keep promising fall on us.

**"if what you say is true!”"** If your claims are true.

### Do people still dare Allah to punish them?

Long after ʿĀd, the disbelievers of Quraysh made the same kind of challenge:

> "And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.”" (8:32).

Daring a messenger to bring on the punishment is the mark of people who have stopped thinking about the consequences of their denial.

### In short

- ʿĀd refused to leave the idols of their forefathers for the worship of Allah alone.
- They mockingly challenged Hūd to bring the punishment he warned of, as Quraysh later did with the Prophet ﷺ.

71.text:
Their provoking answer called for a fitting reply from the Prophet Hūd, including the news that the punishment they asked for would soon come: "He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”" Yet he was a prophet. His fatherly love and wish for their good made him express regret that they worshipped lifeless, senseless things without any proof from reason or revelation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath."** The word for torment is rijs. Ibn ʿAbbās said rijs means scorn and anger. You deserve it from your Lord because of what you have said. It has already been decreed for you and is on its way. Given your defiance and lack of sense, Allah's wrath and punishment are not far off, and may come sooner than you expect.

**"Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods"**: literally "names". Do you argue with me about the idols that you have made gods? Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said Hūd's people worshipped several idols, such as Ṣudāʾ, Ṣamūd and al-Habāʾ.

**"which you and your forefathers have made up"**: you and your fathers called them gods, though they bring neither harm nor benefit and have no basis.

**"a practice Allah has never authorized?"** Did Allah give you any authority, any scripture or decisive proof, allowing you to worship them? He has sent down no proof of their divinity. They had grown so attached to falsehood that they quarrelled with Allah's prophet over it.

**"Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”"** Wait for the punishment you ask for, as you wait for my ruin, and I will wait for yours. It is surely coming. With these words the Messenger threatened and warned his people. Then, because they denied him, a blighting wind was sent against them.

### How do mere names become objects of devotion?

People picture virtues and powers through names. When a good word is attached to someone, he seems good, and when a bad word is attached, he seems bad. Beings other than Allah become the focus of people's devotion through names like these. Some individuals are given titles such as mushkil kusha (solver of difficulties) or ghaus-e-pak (holy hearer of pleas). Others are called gharib nawaz, the benefactor of the poor, or ganj bakhsh, the granter of treasure. Over time the names cling so closely to these figures that people come to believe it. The one called ghaus can really hear their pleas, they think, and the one called mushkil kusha can really solve their problems. Yet all such names are human inventions. No real being bears them, and no religious or rational argument supports them.

That is the form this tradition takes among the ignorant masses. It has a refined form too, popular among the educated. There as well, extraordinary words are attached to certain figures. One is hailed as najat dehenda-e-millat, "saviour of the community", or sutun-e-Islam, "pillar of Islam". Another is called mahbub-e-khuda, "beloved of God", or qudsi sifat, "angelic in nature". Gradually these words become part of the persons' names, and people come to think them as extraordinary as their titles suggest.

Whatever has gained the holiness of the past through long custom looks grand and lofty to people. Beside it, the call of today's preacher seems trivial, so they ignore him as unimportant. They feel sure nothing can harm them, since they think of themselves as heirs to their forefathers' glory. Recklessness toward Allah slowly makes a person numb. He can no longer be reformed by warning or reminder. Only when he hears Allah's voice pronouncing the verdict of punishment will he wake up to his own failings.

### In short

- Hūd told ʿĀd that Allah's wrath and punishment were already decreed for them and close at hand.
- He rebuked them for arguing over idols that were mere names, which Allah had never authorised.
- Grand titles given to created beings can come to be treated as real powers, though they are human inventions.
- Reverence for the past makes people dismiss the present caller, until Allah's verdict wakes them too late.

72.text:
The long struggle of the Prophet Hūd against ʿĀd's stubbornness ended this way: "So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs. They were not believers". Hūd and his believing followers were shielded from the punishment, while the people of ʿĀd who denied him were destroyed root and all.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy"**: Allah saved Hūd and the believers with him, through a mercy from Him.

**"and uprooted those who denied Our signs."** He destroyed and wiped out those who denied His Scripture and His messenger Hūd. Some commentators say this means that everyone alive at the time was destroyed. Others say it means Allah also cut off ʿĀd's line for the future.

**"They were not believers"**: all who were destroyed were disbelievers who deserved their punishment for their denial. Grammatically, "they were not believers" is joined to "those who denied".

### How were ʿĀd destroyed?

Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said that ʿĀd lived in Yemen between Oman and Ḥaḍramawt. They spread through the land and overpowered other peoples with the strength Allah had given them. They worshipped idols instead of Allah, and Allah sent them Hūd, who was of the heart of their lineage and the best of them in standing. Hūd told them to worship Allah alone, to join no partner with Him and to stop wronging people. They rejected him, ignored his call and said, "Who is stronger than us?" A few followed him, but they had to hide their faith. ʿĀd defied Allah's command, denied His prophet and spread corruption in the land. They grew arrogant and built lofty palaces on every height, with no real benefit to themselves. Hūd said to them:

> "˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever and act so viciously when you attack ˹others˺? So fear Allah, and obey me" (26:128-131).

His closing words were a call to taqwā, the fear of Allah, and to obedience.

They answered him, and he answered back:

> "They argued, “O Hûd! You have not given us any clear proof, and we will never abandon our gods upon your word, nor will we believe in you. All we can say is that some of our gods have possessed you with evil.” He said, “I call Allah to witness, and you too bear witness, that I ˹totally˺ reject whatever you associate with Him ˹in worship˺. So let all of you plot against me without delay. I have put my trust in Allah—my Lord and your Lord. There is no living creature that is not completely under His control. Surely my Lord’s Way is perfect justice" (11:53-56).

The Qur'an mentions several times that Allah destroyed ʿĀd with a barren wind that ruined everything it passed over:

> "And as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees. Do you see any of them left alive" (69:6-8).

The wind levelled whatever was left of their gardens, mansions and palaces. It lifted them one by one into the air and brought each down on his head, smashing it and severing it from the body. That is why Allah says they lay "like trunks of uprooted palm trees" (69:7). So ʿĀd were wiped out to the last man.

### Who was the emissary of ʿĀd?

Imam Aḥmad recorded that al-Ḥārith al-Bakrī set out to complain to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. At ar-Rabdhah he met an old woman of Banū Tamīm, alone, who asked him to take her to the Prophet ﷺ about a need of hers. He brought her to Madinah. There he found the mosque full of people, a black flag raised, and Bilāl standing with a sword before the Prophet ﷺ. The people told him the Prophet ﷺ was about to send ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ on an expedition. Later al-Ḥārith was given leave to enter and greeted the Prophet ﷺ, who asked whether there had been a dispute between his tribe and Banū Tamīm. Al-Ḥārith said there had, and that his side had won. He mentioned the old woman, who was waiting at the door, and the Prophet ﷺ let her in.

Al-Ḥārith then asked the Prophet ﷺ to set a barrier between them and Banū Tamīm, such as the desert of ad-Dahnāʾ. The old woman grew angry and objected. Al-Ḥārith said he was like the sheep that carried its own death. He had brought this woman along without knowing she would turn against him. He sought refuge with Allah and His Messenger from being like the emissary of ʿĀd.

The Prophet ﷺ asked him about the emissary of ʿĀd. He knew the story better, but liked to hear it told. Al-Ḥārith said that ʿĀd once suffered a famine and sent an emissary named Qayl to seek relief. Qayl stayed a month with Muʿāwiyah ibn Bakr, who gave him wine while two singing girls sang for him. When the month was over, Qayl went to the mountains of Muhrah. He told Allah that He knew he had not come to cure a sick man or ransom a captive, and asked Him to give ʿĀd water as He used to. Black clouds appeared, and a voice told him to choose one. He pointed to one of the black clouds. Then he heard a voice from it say, "Take it as ashes, leaving no one of ʿĀd." Al-Ḥārith added that he had heard that the wind sent against them was no more than would pass through his ring, yet it destroyed them.

Abū Wāʾil said this was true. When a man or woman sent an emissary, they would tell him, "Do not be like the emissary of ʿĀd," meaning one who brings ruin instead of relief. Imam Aḥmad collected this story in his Musnad, and at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded it in similar wording.

### What lessons does Hūd's story leave?

Here Allah shows how He saved His messenger and the believers and destroyed their stubborn enemies. The story is full of counsel. It reminds heedless people to keep remembering Allah and to live a life of obedience to Him. It shows those who reject sincere advice and refuse to learn what end awaits them. And for preachers and reformers, it is a mirror of the prophetic way of conveying the message (tablīgh) and setting things right (iṣlāḥ).

### In short

- Allah saved Hūd and the believers by His mercy and wiped out ʿĀd, who persisted in denial.
- They built lofty palaces in vanity, oppressed others, and dismissed Hūd's call to taqwā as madness sent by their gods.
- A barren wind blew for seven nights and eight days and hurled them down like uprooted palm trunks.
- "Do not be like the emissary of ʿĀd" became a byword for an envoy who brings ruin instead of relief.
- The story teaches remembrance of Allah, warns those who reject advice, and models the prophetic method for those who call to Allah.

73.text:
After Nūḥ (Noah) and the people of ʿĀd comes the story of the Prophet Ṣāliḥ and his people, Thamūd: "And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ." He told them, "O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord". The proof was a camel: "this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment". Accounts like this one, of earlier prophets calling their peoples to the truth, the peoples' denial and the terrible results, remain the main subject up to the end of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ."** In the Arabic, Thamūda is read without full declension, as the name of the tribe itself. Ṣāliḥ was their prophet. In lineage and homeland he was one of Thamūd, also descended from Sām, so the Qur'an calls him their brother. One explanation says he was their brother in lineage but not in religion.

**"He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him."** Declare Allah's oneness and worship Him alone. You have no god worthy of worship but the One I call you to believe in. Every messenger of Allah, sent to every ummah, called to the worship of Allah alone without partners, as Allah says in other āyāt:

> "We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.”" (21:25).

> "We surely sent a messenger to every community, saying, “Worship Allah and shun false gods.”" (16:36).

Ṣāliḥ's call to his people was no different from the call every messenger has made, from Ādam (Adam) to the last of them.

**"A clear proof has come to you from your Lord"**: a miracle from Allah testifying to the truth of what I have brought you. It is a plain sign of my truthfulness.

**"this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you."** In the Arabic, "a sign to you" describes the state of the camel, governed by the force of "this". She is called "Allah's she-camel" because she was a proof of Allah's perfect power. She appeared in an extraordinary way as a miracle of Ṣāliḥ, a sign of Allah's message. They had asked him to bring her out of a particular rock they had chosen.

**"So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land"**: let her eat its grass unhindered. The words "Allah's land" show that she was to be left free to eat and drink. What she ate and drank did not belong to them. The earth was Allah's, and He created what grew in it.

**"and do not harm her"**: do not touch her with any harm, whether by hamstringing her or by beating her.

**"or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment"**: if you hurt her, a painful punishment will seize you.

### Who were Thamūd, and where did they live?

According to the scholars of tafsīr and genealogy, Thamūd's ancestor was a man of the same name whose line ran back through ʿĀthir, Iram and Sām to Nūḥ. He was the brother of Jadīs son of ʿĀthir, and the tribe of Ṭasm was related to them. They were among the ancient Arabs, al-ʿĀribah, who lived before the time of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and Thamūd came after ʿĀd. As explained in the story of ʿĀd, ʿĀd and Thamūd were two men descended from the same grandfather. Their descendants took their names and became two separate peoples.

Thamūd lived in north-western Arabia, between the Ḥijāz and ash-Shām (Greater Syria). Their main city was called al-Ḥijr, known today as Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ. Like ʿĀd, they were wealthy, powerful, brave and artistically gifted, skilled in sculpture and architecture. They built palaces on open ground and carved dwellings and structures into the mountains. In his book ʿArḍ al-Qurʾān, Maulānā Sayyid Sulaimān Nadvī says their monuments still stand, carved with Iramic and Thamudic inscriptions.

After ʿĀd were destroyed, some righteous people whom Allah had saved settled in al-Ḥijr. Their numbers grew, and they made great progress in farming and building. But later they fell prey to the evils that usually follow material progress and comfort: debauchery, forgetfulness of the Hereafter, disregard for Allah's limits, self-conceit and contempt for Allah's greatness.

Wealth and luxury usually draw people away from the remembrance of their Creator and their final meeting with Him, and push them onto the paths of error. So it was with Thamūd. The world had not forgotten the Flood of Nūḥ, and for Thamūd the destruction of their kin, the people of ʿĀd, was within living memory. Yet riches and might exert their own pull. No sooner does one proud structure collapse than another person or group builds a higher one on the same foundation, ignoring what happened before. When ʿĀd were destroyed, Thamūd inherited their mansions and lands. They put up their places of luxury on the very spots where their kin had perished, and began doing the same deeds. They forgot their Creator and the Hereafter and sank into idol worship and shirk. So Allah, as is His constant way, sent Ṣāliḥ as His messenger to guide them to the straight path.

### What happened at al-Ḥijr?

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by the land and ruins of Thamūd on his way to Tabūk, in northern Arabia, in the ninth year after the hijrah. Imam Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that when the Prophet ﷺ reached al-Ḥijr with the people, he camped near the homes of Thamūd. The people drew water from the wells Thamūd had used, made dough with it and set their cooking pots on the fire. The Prophet ﷺ ordered them to empty the pots and feed the dough to their camels. Then he led them to another spot, near the well from which the she-camel used to drink. He forbade his Companions to enter the place where people had been punished, saying he feared that what struck them might strike them too.

Aḥmad also recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that, in al-Ḥijr, the Prophet ﷺ told the people not to enter the dwellings of those who had been punished unless they were weeping. If they were not weeping, they should not go in, lest what struck those people strike them as well. The core of this hadith is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

### How did the she-camel appear?

Ṣāliḥ began preaching as a young man and kept at it until signs of old age appeared on him, yet he did not give up. His people grew tired of his repeated calls to believe in One God. So they decided to make a demand they thought impossible to meet, so that they would win the contest. They chose a lone, solid rock in the region of al-Ḥijr called al-Katibah. If he really was Allah's messenger, they said, let him bring out of that rock a she-camel in the tenth month of pregnancy, strong and healthy.

First Ṣāliḥ took their pledge. If he met their demand, would they all believe in him and his call? When they had all given their word, he prayed two rakʿahs of ṣalāh. Then he called on Allah, saying that nothing was hard for Him and asking Him to grant their demand. Soon after the supplication the rock rumbled, moved and split apart. Out came a she-camel with a thick coat, pregnant, with her unborn young visibly moving inside her, exactly as they had asked.

At this astonishing miracle some believed at once, among them their chief, Jundaʿ ibn ʿAmr, and several who followed him. The other nobles of Thamūd wanted to believe too. Three men held them back: Rabbāb ibn Ṣumʿar ibn Jilhis, Dhuʾāb ibn ʿAmr ibn Labīd, and al-Ḥabbāb, the keeper of their idols. These chiefs were the real champions of idol worship. A cousin of Jundaʿ named Shihāb ibn Khalīfah ibn Mikhlāt ibn Labīd ibn Jawwās, one of Thamūd's leaders, also wanted to accept the message, but they talked him out of it and he gave in.

When Ṣāliḥ saw that his people had broken their pledge, he feared they would be punished for it. Out of concern for them he urged them not to harm the she-camel in any way and to protect her. Then they might stay safe. Otherwise punishment could seize them at once. That is what this verse says.

### How was the water shared?

The she-camel stayed among Thamūd, and so did the young she gave birth to before their eyes. She drank from the same well that Thamūd used, and because she was an extraordinary creature of Allah, she drank a lot of water, emptying the well. By Allah's will, Ṣāliḥ ruled that she would drink from the well one day and the people the next. On the days she drank, they milked her instead, and filled their water vessels with her milk. Allah refers to this division of water elsewhere:

> "And tell them that the ˹drinking˺ water must be divided between them ˹and her˺, each taking a turn to drink ˹every other day˺.”" (54:28).

The division was to be watched over by angels, so that no one would break it. Another verse says, "Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink as you have yours, each on an appointed day" (26:155).

She grazed in some of their valleys, entering by one pass and leaving by another, so that she could move easily. She was a huge animal of striking beauty, and their cattle took fright whenever she passed.

### Why a she-camel and not a lion?

To test the people of Thamūd, Allah gave them a she-camel and commanded them not to harm her, or they would be destroyed. Allah could just as well have appointed a fearsome lion for the purpose. But He chose a she-camel. The reason is that a person's fear of Allah is always tested at the level of a "she-camel", never at the level of a "lion".

In every society there are people like Allah's she-camel. They are the weak, who have no worldly strength to deter anyone from wronging them. Through them Allah tests the true faith of His servants, and the certificates of Paradise and Hell are issued on the results of these tests. In a universe where everything lives in full obedience to Allah, Thamūd chose to live in arrogance and disobedience. Where everything keeps to the limits Allah has set, they wanted to live by overstepping them. Their transgression spread disorder in a world that had been set right, so they were judged unfit to live in it.

### In short

- Allah sent Ṣāliḥ, their brother by descent, to Thamūd of al-Ḥijr in north-western Arabia, with the same call as every messenger: worship Allah alone.
- At their demand, Allah brought a pregnant she-camel out of the rock al-Katibah as a clear sign. Yet their chiefs kept most of them from believing.
- The well was shared by turns, and they were warned that harming the camel would bring a painful punishment.
- At al-Ḥijr the Prophet ﷺ forbade using Thamūd's water and told the Companions to pass the ruins only in tears.
- Faith is tested by how people treat the weak, Allah's "she-camels", not the strong.

74.text:
Out of concern for these stubborn, pledge-breaking people, Ṣāliḥ reminds them of Allah's favours, hoping they will soften: "Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land—˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains and carved homes into mountains. So remember Allah’s favours, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”" After destroying ʿĀd, Allah settled Thamūd in their place, gave them ʿĀd's lands and homes, and granted them the skill to build great palaces and carve whole dwellings out of mountains.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd"**: the word khulafāʾ is the plural of khalīfah, a successor or deputy. Praise Allah for making you successors on earth after the destruction of the people of ʿĀd, who persisted in disbelief.

**"and established you in the land"**: He settled you there, so that you could enjoy it and meet your needs.

**"˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains"**: quṣūr is the plural of qaṣr, a palace or grand building. They built palaces on the plains out of the plains' own clay, and lived in them in summer.

**"and carved homes into mountains."** Tanḥitūn comes from naḥt, carving stone. Jibāl is the plural of jabal, a mountain, and buyūt the plural of bayt, a house or its rooms. They hewed houses out of the mountains to live in during winter. In the Arabic, "homes" is in the accusative because of an implied word describing a state.

**"So remember Allah’s favours"**: remember Allah's blessings, thank Him for them and believe in Him.

**"and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”"** Do not wreck the earth with disbelief and disobedience, or by calling people to other than Allah. Do not put your efforts into corruption.

### Was their progress the problem?

Thamūd brought the art of building to perfection. They must have been well versed in related sciences such as mathematics, geometry and engineering, or such development would have been impossible. Yet they were not condemned for material progress. They were condemned for spreading corruption on earth. This shows that Allah does not forbid progress within lawful limits. But in the way he lives, a person should follow the balance that Allah has set throughout the universe.

### What rulings come from this verse?

Some basic and secondary rulings follow from this verse.

1. All the prophets agree on the fundamental articles of faith, and their codes of law are united in the same way. All of them call to tawḥīd, pure monotheism, as the basis of worshipping Allah. All of them warn that going against it brings punishment in this world and the next.
2. In earlier peoples too, the wealthy and the traditional holders of social standing refused the prophets' call. They were disgraced and destroyed in this world, and they deserve punishment in the Hereafter.
3. According to Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, the verse shows that Allah's worldly blessings reach disbelievers too, as with ʿĀd and Thamūd, to whom He gave great wealth and power.
4. According to al-Qurṭubī again, the verse shows that palaces and mansions are blessings from Allah, and building them is permissible.

It is another matter that the noble prophets and the friends of Allah did not favour such buildings, because they make people heedless. The sayings of the Prophet ﷺ about tall buildings are of this kind.

### In short

- Ṣāliḥ reminded Thamūd that Allah made them successors to ʿĀd and gave them the skill to build palaces and carve homes into mountains.
- They were condemned not for their progress but for spreading corruption. Progress within Allah's limits is allowed.
- All prophets share one creed, and the wealthy and powerful have often been the first to reject them.
- Building palaces is permissible, though the prophets and the friends of Allah avoided them for the heedlessness they bring.

75.text:
Thamūd split into two groups, and the verse records their exchange: "The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them, “Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?” They replied, “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”" One group had come to believe that Ṣāliḥ was a prophet, and the other denied and disbelieved.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant chiefs of his people"**: the leaders and important people who were too proud to believe in him.

**"asked the lowly who believed among them"**: literally "those who were made weak". They spoke to those they had overpowered and looked down on as weak, the believers among them. In the Arabic, "to such of them as believed" restates "to those who were made weak", repeating the preposition "to".

**"“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”"** Do you really know that Ṣāliḥ is a messenger to you from his Lord?

**"They replied, “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”"** Yes, we believe firmly in the message he was sent with, and we act on what he has brought us.

### Why "the arrogant" but "the weakened"?

Imam Rāzī says in Tafsīr Kabīr that the Qur'an names a quality of each group here, but in different forms. The disbelievers' quality is in the active voice: "who were arrogant". The believers' state is in the passive: "who were made weak". This shows that the disbelievers' arrogance was their own choice, blameworthy and the final cause of their punishment. The weakness and lowliness of the believers, on the other hand, was only how the disbelievers described them. It had nothing to do with the believers' real state, and nothing in it was blameworthy at all. Those to blame are the ones who called them weak and lowly, and treated them so, without any reason.

### What made the believers' answer so apt?

The well-known Tafsīr Kashshāf says it was a most eloquent answer. In effect they said: your whole debate, whether he is Allah's messenger or not, is not worth having. That is plain, settled and certain. Just as certain is that what he says is a message from Allah. If anything is worth discussing, it is who believes in him and who does not. As for us, praise be to Allah, we believe in every word of guidance he has brought.

A prophet usually appears in his own time as a controversial figure, not an established personality. No worldly glory surrounds him, and he holds none of the important positions of his day. So his contemporaries cannot see his prophethood and reject him. They find it hard to believe that the man they know as ordinary is the very one Allah has chosen to deliver His message.

The reply of Ṣāliḥ's companions shows the difference between the two groups. The deniers looked at Ṣāliḥ's person, while the believers looked at his message. The deniers saw no outward glory around him, so they ignored him. The believers saw the light of truth in his message, so they accepted his words at once and became his companions.

### In short

- The arrogant chiefs challenged the humble believers to say whether they were sure Ṣāliḥ was sent by Allah.
- The believers answered that his messengership was beyond debate. The only question was who believed, and they did.
- The Qur'an calls the disbelievers' arrogance their own choice, while the believers' "weakness" was only the label the arrogant gave them.
- The deniers judged the messenger's person and status, while the believers judged the truth of his message.

76.text:
Even that eloquent answer could not soften the disbelievers of Thamūd: "The arrogant said, “We surely reject what you believe in.”" They answered coldly and proudly that they rejected what the believers had accepted.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant said"**: those who were too proud to believe.

**"“We surely reject what you believe in.”"** We deny what you have faith in, O believers. We will not believe in it, and we will not act on its sacred laws.

### Why could they not see what was plain?

The lust for worldly life is merciless, and so is the poisonous thrill of wealth and power. May Allah protect us all from them, for they become invisible curtains before human eyes. They stop eyes that can see from seeing what is obvious.

Truth always shows itself through the strength of its arguments, not through worldly glory. Those who can see truth in the form of argument find it at once. Those forever dazzled by outward glory remain in doubt. They are never granted the guidance to become supporters of the truth.

### In short

- The arrogant of Thamūd flatly rejected everything the believers had accepted.
- Love of the world and the intoxication of wealth and power blind people to what is plain.
- Truth appears through argument, not glory. Those dazzled by glory stay in doubt and are left without guidance.

77.text:
The she-camel had become Thamūd's final test, and they failed it: "Then they killed the she-camel—defying their Lord’s command—and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”" The camel drank on one day and they on the next, and they soon grew tired of the arrangement. They wanted her gone, but they did not dare kill her themselves for fear of divine punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then they killed the she-camel"**: literally "they hamstrung her". Qudār hamstrung her at their command and killed her with a sword. She was the camel they had been forbidden to touch with harm.

**"defying their Lord’s command"**: they insolently refused the commands of their Lord that Ṣāliḥ had given them, too proud to obey.

**"and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with"**: O Ṣāliḥ, bring on us the painful punishment you promised for killing her.

**"if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”"** They said this in mockery, doubting what he had told them would happen.

### Who killed the she-camel?

As this went on, and Thamūd's rejection of Ṣāliḥ grew more bitter, they decided to kill the camel so that they could have the water every day. It is said that the whole of disbelieving Thamūd conspired in it. Qatādah said he was told that the man chosen to kill the camel went round to all of them, even the women in their rooms and the children, and found that everyone agreed. The wording of the verses shows this:

> "Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their crime, levelling all to the ground" (91:14).

> "And We gave Thamûd the she-camel as a clear sign, but they wrongfully rejected it" (17:59).

Here too the verse says "they killed the she-camel". These verses state that the whole tribe shared in agreeing to the crime, and Allah knows best.

Shayṭān has endless weapons. One of his deadliest tricks, which strips people of whatever sense they have, is temptation through women. Imam Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Jarīr and other scholars of tafsīr said the killing began with a disbelieving old woman named Umm Ghanm ʿUnayzah, daughter of Ghanm ibn Mijlaz. She had the fiercest hatred of Ṣāliḥ in all Thamūd. She was wealthy, had beautiful daughters, and was married to Dhuʾāb ibn ʿAmr, one of Thamūd's leaders. Another noblewoman, Ṣadūf, daughter of al-Muḥayyā ibn Dahr ibn al-Muḥayyā, was of noble family, wealthy and beautiful. She had been married to a Muslim man of Thamūd but had left him.

These two women offered a prize to whoever swore to kill the camel: he could have one of them, or one of their daughters. Al-Ḥabbāb was the first man Ṣadūf approached. She offered herself to him as the reward, but he would not do it. So she called her cousin Muṣaddiʿ ibn Mihrāj ibn al-Muḥayyā, and he agreed. ʿUnayzah called Qudār ibn Sālif ibn Jundaʿ, a short man with reddish-blue skin. They said he was illegitimate, the son not of Sālif but of a man named Suhyād, though born in Sālif's house. ʿUnayzah promised him any of her daughters he wished if he killed the camel. In one telling, the two young men are named Misdaʿ and Qadhār.

Qudār and Muṣaddiʿ recruited several troublemakers of Thamūd. Seven more agreed, making nine, as Allah describes:

> "And there were in the city nine ˹elite˺ men who spread corruption in the land, never doing what is right" (27:48).

These nine were chiefs of their people, and they drew the whole tribe into agreeing to the killing. They waited until the camel left the well. Qudār hid beside a rock on her path and Muṣaddiʿ behind another. As she passed Muṣaddiʿ, he shot an arrow that pierced her leg. Then ʿUnayzah came out and had her daughter, one of the most beautiful of women, uncover her face to spur Qudār on. He struck the camel's leg with his sword and she fell. She let out a single cry to warn her young. Then Qudār stabbed her in the neck and slaughtered her.

Her young one climbed a high rock and cried out. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq recorded from Maʿmar, through someone who reported it from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣarī, that the young one said, "My Lord, where is my mother?" It is said that it cried out three times, then entered a rock and vanished into it. Others say they chased it and killed it with its mother. Allah knows best. The Qur'an calls the killer the most wretched of Thamūd: "when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺" (91:12). That deed brought punishment on the whole people.

### What did Ṣāliḥ say, and what did they plot?

When the news reached Ṣāliḥ, he came to them as they were gathered. Seeing the camel, he wept. As Allah commanded, he told them they had only three days left:

> "But they killed her, so he warned ˹them˺, “You have ˹only˺ three ˹more˺ days to enjoy life in your homes—this is an unfailing promise!”" (11:65).

But when a people's ruin falls due, no advice or warning works. Even Ṣāliḥ's honest counsel had no effect. Instead they mocked him, asking how and from where the punishment would come, and what its signs would be.

The nine wicked men had killed the camel on a Wednesday. That night they plotted to kill Ṣāliḥ. Their reasoning was this: if he was truthful, they should finish him before they were finished, and if he was a liar, let him follow his camel. They swore by Allah to attack him and his family by night. Afterwards they would tell his heirs that they had not witnessed the killing and were telling the truth (27:49-50). Allah says:

> "And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware" (27:50).

They gathered by night to carry out their plot. But Allah, who has all might and protects His messengers, rained down stones that smashed the heads of those nine before the rest of the tribe could act. They were struck down by the hail of stones while still on their way to his house.

### Is everyone guilty when one person sins?

The one who killed Ṣāliḥ's she-camel was a single arrogant member of the community. Yet the act is credited to them all: "they killed the she-camel". This shows that when one member of a group does an evil deed and the others do not condemn it, all of them are counted as parties to the crime.

### In short

- Tired of sharing the water, Thamūd agreed as a whole people to kill the she-camel, though only a few did the deed.
- Two women offered themselves and their daughters as a prize. Qudār and Muṣaddiʿ, with seven others, ambushed and killed the camel.
- Ṣāliḥ gave them three days. They mocked him and plotted to kill him by night, but Allah destroyed the nine plotters with stones.
- A crime done by one and approved by the rest is counted against them all.

78.text:
The promised punishment arrived: "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes". The word ar-rajfah means an earthquake.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them"**: a violent earthquake seized them, along with a loud cry from the sky announcing their punishment. It came when the punishment they had asked for arrived.

**"and they fell lifeless in their homes"**: the word is jāthimīn. It comes from juthūm, which means being struck senseless and motionless in one spot, or remaining seated, as Al-Qāmūs explains. It is also likened to a dead bird that lands on its breast. They lay dead wherever they were, fallen on their faces and knees, keeled over, without a movement, in their town. Not one of them escaped. We seek refuge with Allah from His wrath and His punishment.

### How did the three days pass?

When they mocked him and asked for signs, Ṣāliḥ told them what would happen. On the next day, Thursday, their faces would turn yellow, every one of them, men and women, young and old. On Friday all their faces would turn red, and on Saturday, the third day, jet black. That day would be the last of their lives.

On Thursday morning, the first day of the respite, their faces turned yellow, as though painted, just as Ṣāliḥ had said. The first sign had come true. Yet these tyrants did not soften enough to believe in Allah and stop their wrongdoing. Their rage against Ṣāliḥ only grew, and everyone ran about trying to find and kill him. May Allah protect everyone from His wrath. It too has its signs, which turn hearts and minds upside down, so that people take gain for loss, loss for gain, good for bad and bad for good.

On Friday, the second day, their faces turned red, as foretold. On Saturday, the third day, they turned black. Now there was nowhere to go. On Sunday they rubbed on ḥanūṭ, the perfume used for shrouding the dead, and in despair waited for Allah's punishment and vengeance. They did not know what would be done to them, or how, or from where it would come.

When the sun rose, the cry came from the sky and a violent tremor shook them from below. The souls were taken and the bodies left lifeless, all within an hour. None of them, young or old, male or female, escaped.

### Was it an earthquake or a cry?

Another verse says, "But the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them in the morning" (15:83). The word aṣ-Ṣaiḥah means a shrill cry or a terrible sound. These two verses show that two punishments struck Thamūd together: the earthquake from below and the cry from above. Its sound killed everyone instantly and at once.

### Did anyone escape?

The scholars of tafsīr said that none of Thamūd's descendants survived except Ṣāliḥ and those who believed in him. A disbelieving man named Abū Righāl was in the Sacred Precinct (Ḥaram) of Makkah at the time, so the punishment that struck his people did not touch him. Allah spared him for the sanctity of the Ḥaram. But one day, when he left the Sacred Precinct, a stone fell from the sky and killed him, the same punishment that had seized his people.

ʿAbd ar-Razzāq reported, through Maʿmar from Ismāʿīl ibn Umayyah, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by Abū Righāl's grave on the outskirts of Makkah. He asked the Companions whether they knew whose grave it was, and they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He told them it was the grave of Abū Righāl, a man of Thamūd. Being in Allah's Sacred Precinct had saved him from the punishment, he said, but when he left it, what struck his people struck him. He had been buried with a branch made of gold. The people dug with their swords, looking for the golden branch, and found it. Some narrations call it a walking stick of gold. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq reported through Maʿmar that az-Zuhrī said Abū Righāl was the ancestor of the tribe of Thaqīf, the people of Ṭāʾif.

### How much of this story is certain?

The important parts of Thamūd's story are told in various surahs of the Qur'an itself, and some parts appear in hadith narrations. Other details were taken by commentators from Israelite narratives. But the truth of the event does not depend on those.

### In short

- After three days of yellow, red and black faces, a violent earthquake from below and a terrible cry from above destroyed Thamūd.
- They fell dead where they were, kneeling and motionless, and none escaped but Ṣāliḥ and the believers.
- Even as the signs came true, their hatred of Ṣāliḥ only grew, a mark of hearts turned upside down by Allah's wrath.
- Abū Righāl escaped while in the Ḥaram of Makkah, but was struck dead when he left it.

79.text:
After the punishment had fallen, Ṣāliḥ turned from his people: "So he turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”" These were words of reproach and blame for a people Allah had destroyed for defying Him, rebelling against Him, refusing the truth, avoiding guidance and preferring error.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So he turned away from them"**: Ṣāliḥ turned his back on them, having given up all hope for them, and left them. One explanation says he left them before they were destroyed. After the punishment, Ṣāliḥ and those who believed in him left that place for somewhere else. Some narrations say four thousand believers went with him to Ḥaḍramawt in Yemen, where he died. Others say he went to Makkah and died there.

**"saying, “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message"**: I delivered what Allah told me to deliver to you, explaining His commands and prohibitions.

**"and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice"**: I advised you well, encouraging and warning you. I warned you of Allah's punishment and called you to repent and believe.

**"but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”"** You did not benefit from my advice, because you do not love the truth and do not follow those who advise you sincerely, who want to lead you to good and away from evil. You do not listen to them.

### Why speak to people who were already dead?

The wording suggests that Ṣāliḥ spoke to his people as he was leaving, after they were destroyed. What use was it to address them then? One benefit is that people in general would learn the lesson. Some say his destroyed people heard him, as a miracle Allah granted to Ṣāliḥ.

The Prophet ﷺ did something similar. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs report that after defeating the disbelievers at Badr he stayed three days, then rode out late at night to the well where their corpses lay. He called out to the dead leaders of Quraysh by name, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām among them, asking whether they had found their Lord's promise true, as he had found his. When ʿUmar asked why he spoke to bodies that had rotted, he swore that they heard him as well as ʿUmar did, though they could not reply.

It is also possible that Ṣāliḥ said these words before the punishment came and his people were destroyed, even though the text places them afterwards.

### Why were the ruins left standing?

On the Tabūk journey, as al-Bukhārī records, the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions not to enter that stricken land and not to use water from its wells. In His infinite wisdom, Allah has let the dwellings of punished peoples stand as signposts of warning for later generations. The Qur'an repeatedly told the people of Arabia that these places, which lay on their trade route to Syria, should drive home the lesson of how nations rise and fall:

> "˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly" (28:58).

### Why do people turn from sincere advisers?

A community that gives in to its desires is not moved by honest talk. It will not stand behind anyone who calls it to serious and sincere effort. Instead, huge crowds gather around those who speak pleasant words and deal in false promises. People are not drawn to their true well-wishers. They rush toward those who exploit them.

### In short

- Ṣāliḥ left his destroyed people, reminding them that he had delivered Allah's message and advised them sincerely.
- He and the believers moved on, to Ḥaḍramawt by most reports, or to Makkah.
- Like the Prophet ﷺ at Badr, he addressed the dead so that the living might learn.
- The ruins of punished peoples remain as warnings, and people who follow their desires prefer flatterers to sincere advisers.

80.text:
