The fourth story in the series is that of the Prophet Lūṭ (Lot): "And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people, ˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before". Allah sent Lūṭ to call his people to His oneness, to command good and to forbid them from their evil practices, their sin and their wickedness.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people"**: and We sent Lūṭ to his people. In the Arabic, "Lūṭan" is explained by the clause that follows, "when he said to his people".

**"˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed"**: the shameful deed was sodomy, unnatural relations between men.

**"that no man has ever done before"**: no creature, human or jinn, in all the worlds had ever done it before them. None of the children of Ādam (Adam) had done it before, nor had it even crossed their minds. ʿAmr ibn Dīnār said that before the people of Lūṭ, no male had ever had relations with another male.

### Who was Lūṭ?

Lūṭ was the son of Hārān, son of Āzar (Terah), and the nephew of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the Friend of Allah and father of the prophets. Both came from the land of Babel, near Basra, in Iraq. Idol worship was common there, and even Ibrāhīm's own family took part in it. Allah sent Ibrāhīm as a prophet to guide them. His people opposed him until matters came to a head with Nimrūd's famous fire, and his own father threatened to throw him out of the house.

Of his whole family, only his wife Sārah and his nephew Lūṭ accepted Islam: "So Lot believed in him" (29:26). With these two Ibrāhīm emigrated to Syria (ash-Shām), leaving his homeland behind. After reaching the River Jordan, he settled in Canaan, near Bayt al-Maqdis, by divine command.

Then Allah made Lūṭ a prophet too, and sent him to guide the people of Sadūm (Sodom), near Bayt al-Maqdis, and the villages around it. The area had five main cities: Sadūm, ʿAmūrah, Admah, Ṣubūyīm and Bāliʿ, also called Ṣawghar. In several places the Qur'an calls them al-Muʾtafikah and al-Muʾtafikāt. Sadūm was their centre and capital, and Lūṭ lived there. The land was fertile and green, rich in every kind of grain and fruit. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and other works give these details.

### How did a prosperous people fall so low?

Allah describes human nature in the Qur'an: "Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds once they think they are self-sufficient" (96:6-7). Allah had opened the doors of His blessings to these people too. Driven by this common pattern and soaked in wealth, they went to the furthest limits of luxury and lust. They lost the most basic human sense of honour, dignity and modesty, and with it the very ability to tell good from bad. So they fell into unnatural indecency. Besides being ḥarām and sinful, such acts are repugnant to anyone of sound and decent taste, so much so that even animals do not go near them.

### Why "the shameful deed"?

When speaking of zinā (adultery), the Qur'an says, "It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way" (17:32). There the word fāḥishah, "a shameful deed", is indefinite. Here it is definite, al-fāḥishah, "the shameful deed". This hints that this unnatural act gathers all indecencies into one, and is a far graver crime than zinā.

The verse also says that no one in all the worlds had done it before them. No one, not even the worst of people, had ever thought of such a thing before the people of Sadūm. The Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik said that had the Qur'an not told of the people of Lūṭ, he would never have imagined that a human being could do such a thing.

### Why is a new sin especially grave?

Their shamelessness is condemned on two grounds.

1. People often fall into sins because of their social conditions, or by blindly following their ancestors. That is no valid excuse in the Sharīʿah, but in ordinary practice such a person may be thought excusable to some degree. A sin that no one has ever committed before, with no special pressure behind it, is a curse of the highest degree.
2. Such an act opens a channel that draws others into the same curse. Whoever invents an evil act or custom bears its sin and punishment himself. He also carries the sin and punishment of everyone who follows his lead, right up to the Last Day.

### The inner reading: each rank has its own indecency

Each person's indecency matches his days and his states. Look at where a person stands on the road of the spiritual journey, and his indecency will be measured to his human nature at that point. People fall into three ranks: the common folk, the chosen few, and the chosen of the chosen.

- For the common folk, indecency is what the Sharīʿah defines, punished by flogging or stoning.
- For the chosen few, it is letting the physical eye linger on this world's pleasures and appetites, on their delight and their glitter, and letting them in, even when they are lawful and free of doubt. For such people the lawful pleasures of this world do more harm than forbidden things do to the common folk. In the words of the Master of the Sharīʿah, the penalty for this indecency is: "Lower your eyes and hold back your hands."
- For the chosen of the chosen, it is turning the heart's attention to anything other than the Real. This is despite the command from the Real: "Say, “Allah ˹revealed it˺!” Then leave them" (6:91).

It is as if He says: My servant, do not look at yourself, but see everything as My act. Do not count your deeds as a favour to Me. Look at the success I give you. Flee from your own traces and see only My love. What has someone seized by His love to do with anyone else? Keep your heart turned toward Him and let the rest go. All the world's uproar is talk of "you" and "me". Give up "me", and the whole world will be your garden. Allah says, "I wonder how anyone who believes in Me can rely on other than Me. If they looked at the fine touches of My kindness, they would worship none but Me."

### In short

- Lūṭ, nephew of Ibrāhīm, emigrated with him to Syria and was sent as a prophet to Sodom and its sister cities near Bayt al-Maqdis.
- Wealth and luxury led the people of Sodom to lose all modesty and invent an unnatural indecency no one had committed before.
- Calling it "the shameful deed" marks it as graver than zinā. Inventing a new sin brings the burden of everyone who follows it.
- In the inner reading, each rank has its own indecency, down to turning the heart toward anything other than Allah.

81.text:
Lūṭ (Lot) then names their deed plainly: "You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”" For the natural fulfilment of human desire, Allah appointed marriage with women as the lawful way. To bypass it for an unnatural way is plain ugliness of the self and proof of a corrupted mind.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You lust after men instead of women!"** You find more desire in men than in the women Allah created for you, the women you were meant to go to. In the Arabic, the question can be read a-innakum, with both hamzahs pronounced, or with the second softened, an alif being inserted between them in both cases. Another reading is innakum, "indeed you". Leaving the women Allah created for them and going to men instead is evil and ignorant behaviour, because it puts things where they do not belong. In doing so they followed neither sense, nor any sound report, nor even nature itself.

**"You are certainly transgressors.”"** You are a people who go beyond the bounds, from the lawful to the unlawful. One explanation adds: and transgressors in idolatry too. Their real disease was that they crossed the limits Allah set for everything. In their case it was the very limit of humanity they leapt over. With sexual desire, too, they crossed the limits Allah appointed in reaching for what goes against nature. Moderation, good sense and the natural dignity of human beings were all left behind.

### How did they answer Lūṭ's reminder?

Lūṭ reminded them of their women: "He said, “O my people! Here are my daughters ˹so marry them˺ if you wish to do so.”" (15:71). They replied that they had no desire for women:

> "They argued, “You certainly know that we have no need for your daughters. You already know what we desire!”" (11:79).

That is, you know we do not want women, and you know what we want with your guests.

### How grave is this sin in Islamic law?

For this reason the Companions, the Successors and the mujtahid imams declared this crime and sin far graver than other acts of shame. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah said its punishment should match the punishment Allah sent on the people of Lūṭ, when stones rained from the sky and the ground was turned upside down. So, he said, the offender should be thrown down from a height and stoned from above.

Imam Aḥmad in his Musnad, Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded a hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās about those who commit this act. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever is found doing the deed of the people of Lūṭ is to be put to death, both the one who does it and the one to whom it is done.

### What is "the reformed state" that they broke?

The universe follows a natural scheme, which the Qur'an calls iṣlāḥ, the reformed state. Going against it upsets the balance of things, which the Qur'an calls fasād. Only human beings misuse their freedom to go against the way of nature, and Lūṭ's people did exactly this to the divine order. The natural form of sexual relationship is between husband and wife, and that is the way of iṣlāḥ. Sexual relations between man and man, or woman and woman, cross the limits Allah has set. That is what the Qur'an calls fasād.

### In short

- Lūṭ condemned his people for turning from the women Allah created for them to men, against nature and sense.
- They were transgressors who leapt over every limit Allah set, even the limit of humanity itself.
- The scholars count this sin graver than other indecencies. Abū Ḥanīfah likened its penalty to the punishment of Lūṭ's people, and a hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās orders death for both parties.
- The natural bond of husband and wife is the way of iṣlāḥ. Turning from it is fasād.

82.text:
His people had no answer to Lūṭ's (Lot's) advice, yet they would not give way: "But his people’s only response was to say, “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”" Instead of reasoning, they turned on the prophet and his followers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But his people’s only response was to say"**: those who committed this shameless deed, which they had been forbidden, simply turned away from the truth. They said to one another what follows.

**"“Expel them from your land!"** Drive Lūṭ and his followers out of your town. One explanation names those meant as Lūṭ and his two daughters, Zaʿūrā and Raythā. They tried to banish him and the believers from their village. In the end Allah brought Lūṭ out safely from among them, and destroyed them in their own land in disgrace and humiliation.

**"They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”"** They want to keep themselves clean of what we do, so it does not suit them to go on living among us. Qatādah said they shamed Lūṭ and the believers with something that is no shame at all. Mujāhid said they meant: these people want to keep themselves clean of the acts we commit with men and with women. Something similar is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

### Why did they want to banish the pure?

They seemed to be saying to each other: these people are self-righteous and claim great purity for themselves, so the treatment they deserve is to be thrown out of town. If they think us dirty and want to stay clean, why should the clean live with the unclean? Let them leave our town.

These words reeked of arrogance. They dared to say them because they were the majority and had worldly power, and so they felt safe. Only a few people close to Lūṭ believed in him, and all the rest were sunk in debauchery.

### In short

- Having no reply to Lūṭ, his people resolved to drive him and his followers out of the town.
- They mocked the believers for wanting to stay pure, making purity itself a charge against them.
- Their boldness came from being the majority with worldly power. Allah saved Lūṭ and destroyed them in disgrace.

83.text:
The fourth and fifth verses of this passage tell of the punishment that fell on the people of Sadūm for their crooked and shameless ways: "So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed". The punishment came on the whole people, except Lūṭ (Lot) and the few with him who were kept safe.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We saved him"**: Allah rescued Lūṭ by telling him to leave the city by night.

**"and his family"**: his household, for only his household believed in him. One explanation names his daughters, Zaʿūrā and Raythā. Allah says elsewhere, "Then ˹before the torment˺ We evacuated the believers from the city. But We only found one family that had submitted ˹to Allah˺" (51:35-36). Who were his "family" (ahl)? Some say they were two women of his household who had become Muslims, and not his wife. The verse just quoted says that in all those settlements there was only one Muslim household (51:36). So only people from Lūṭ's household were saved, not including his wife. Others say ahl is general here. It includes his own family and others who had joined him by accepting Islam. Either way, they were a small number of Muslims. To save them, Allah ordered Lūṭ to take them, without his wife, and leave the town late at night without looking back. Once they were out, the punishment would fall at once on those inside.

**"except his wife"**: of his family, only his wife did not believe. She stayed on her people's religion. She plotted with them against Lūṭ and let them know who came to visit him, using signals they had agreed on. That is why, when Lūṭ was ordered to leave by night with his family, he was told not to inform his wife or take her with him.

**"who was one of the doomed"**: the word is al-ghābirīn. It means those who stayed behind, or those who were destroyed. The second is the more obvious meaning. She remained in the city and suffered the same punishment as the rest.

### What happened to Lūṭ's wife?

Lūṭ followed the divine command and left Sadūm late at night with his family and companions. There are two reports about his wife. One says she simply did not go with them. The other says she did set out with them and walked for a while. But she was eager to see what became of the people she had left behind, and she looked back, against the command. Then the punishment seized her as it seized them. It appears more likely that she never left the town, and that Lūṭ did not tell her they were leaving, so she remained with her people. This event is told in the Qur'an on several occasions in varying detail. Here it is said briefly that Allah saved Lūṭ and his family and companions, while his wife was left to share the punishment.

### Can kinship save anyone from Allah's judgement?

The prophet Lūṭ's own wife was among those destroyed. This shows Allah's impartial justice in reward and punishment. In Allah's scales, family ties and friendships count for nothing. His judgement was so impartial that it did not spare Nūḥ's (Noah's) son, Ibrāhīm's (Abraham's) father, Lūṭ's wife or the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. On the other hand, Pharaoh's wife did righteous deeds and was admitted to Paradise.

### In short

- Allah saved Lūṭ and the few believers of his household by having them leave the city by night without looking back.
- His wife, who plotted with her people and betrayed his guests, was left behind and destroyed with them.
- Kinship with a prophet saves no one, and a tyrant's believing wife can reach Paradise.

84.text:
The punishment is described here in a few words: "We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked". An extraordinary rain was sent upon them, and its details are given in Sūrah Hūd.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺."** Allah sent down on them stones from the sky, stones of baked clay (ḥijārat as-sijjīl), which destroyed them. One explanation says they fell on their travellers as well as on the rest. Another verse explains this rain:

> "When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay, marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers" (11:82-83).

**"See what was the end of the wicked"**: look, O Muhammad, at how it ended for people who dared to defy Allah and deny His messengers. Their end was destruction, ruin and lasting disgrace.

### How did the punishment unfold?

The verses of Sūrah Hūd show that stones rained from above, while from below Jibrāʾīl raised the entire surface of the land and flung it back down, overturned. The stones fell one upon another, so relentlessly that they piled up in layers. They were marked, and some commentators say each stone bore the name of the person it was to destroy. Allah overturned the city and turned it upside down.

Sūrat al-Ḥijr mentions, before the account of the punishment, "So the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise" (15:73). This suggests that a harsh sound from the sky came first, and then the other punishments. The order of the words suggests that after this blast the earth was turned upside down, and then stones rained on them to seal their disgrace. It is also possible that the stones came first and the overturning later, since in the Qur'an's style what is mentioned first need not have happened first.

Of all the terrible punishments sent on Lūṭ's people, the overturning of the earth fits their deed in a particular way, because they were guilty of turning nature upside down.

### Can the place still be seen?

At the end of the verses from Sūrah Hūd quoted above, the Qur'an warns the people of Arabia that these overturned cities "are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers". They passed by them on their journeys to Syria, and it is surprising that they learnt no lesson.

These sights did not vanish with the age of revelation. They are still there, between Bayt al-Maqdis and the River Jordan, above all around the Dead Sea, which is also called the Sea of Lūṭ. It lies far below sea level. In one part its water is unusual, and no sea creature can live in it, hence the name Dead Sea. Here, it is said, stood Sodom of old. We ask Allah to protect us from His punishment and His anger.

The ruling on this crime, reported in the hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās, has been given under 7:81.

### In short

- Allah rained marked stones of baked clay on the people of Lūṭ, turned their cities upside down, and struck them with a mighty blast at sunrise.
- Overturning the earth matched their crime of overturning nature.
- The site, by the Dead Sea between Bayt al-Maqdis and the Jordan, remains a warning on the old route to Syria.

85.text:
The fifth story is that of the Prophet Shuʿayb and his people: "And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib." His message began, "O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord." Then came its demands: "So give just measure and weight, do not defraud people of their property, nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers". His people were cheating in trade and making the land a place of disorder, and he came to set them right.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib."** He was their prophet. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said the people of Madyan descended from Madyan, son of Ibrāhīm (Abraham). He also said that Shuʿayb was the son of Mīkīl ibn Yashjur, that his name in Syriac was Yathrūn (Jethro), and that he was related to Lūṭ (Lot). Madyan was the name of the tribe and also of a city, near Maʿān on the road from ash-Shām to the Ḥijāz. When the Qur'an tells the story of Mūsā (Moses) elsewhere, it says, "When he arrived at the well of Midian, he found a group of people watering ˹their herds˺" (28:23). It refers to this same place.

**"He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him."** Declare Allah's oneness and worship Him alone. This is the call of all the messengers. These people too had given themselves over to worshipping created things, forgetting the Being and attributes of Allah and neglecting His rights, so this was the first message given to them.

**"A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord."** Allah has set before you the proofs and evidence of the truth of what I have brought. The clear proofs are the miracles that appeared at Shuʿayb's hands, and Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ describes the forms they took.

**"So give just measure and weight"**: kayl means measure and mīzān means weighing. Give people their rights by measuring and weighing correctly.

**"do not defraud people of their property"**: bakhs means causing someone loss by giving him less than his due. Do not cheat people in buying and selling, or run down their goods to short-change them. They used to treacherously avoid giving full weight and measure. The first part of the verse forbids the particular crime of short measure and short weight. These words then widen the ban to every kind of cutting down, trimming or short-changing of rights, whether in property, honour or anything else. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ explains it this way.

**"nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order."** Do not corrupt the earth with disbelief, disobedience, calling people to other than Allah and giving short measure. It was set right by the sending of messengers, by acts of obedience and by fair measure. The same phrase came earlier in this surah, at 7:56. The physical good order of the earth depends on using things rightly, keeping limits and holding to moderation, fairness and justice. Its spiritual good order depends on a bond with Allah and obedience to His commands. Physical and spiritual disorder appear when these principles are weakened or abandoned. Shuʿayb's people had abandoned them completely, turning the earth into a hotbed of disorder. So they were told to stop deeds that spread corruption through the whole earth.

**"This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers"**: declaring Allah's oneness and giving full measure and weight are better for you than your present ways, if you believe what I tell you. If you are seeking faith, hurry to it. If they repented and turned from their evil, only good awaited them, in this life and the next. Success in the Hereafter plainly depends on obeying Allah's commands. In this world too, once people find someone honest in weights and measures and careful of all his customers' rights, his credit and goodwill are established in the market. His trade grows in size and reliability.

### Who were the people of Madyan and al-Aykah?

The Qur'an calls the people to whom Shuʿayb was sent both the people of Madyan and the people of al-Aykah. Al-Aykah means a forest or thicket.

Some commentators say these were two different peoples living in separate settlements. Shuʿayb was sent to one of them first, and when they were destroyed, to the other. Their punishments are also described in different words. The punishment of Madyan is called aṣ-Ṣaiḥah, the blast, in some places and ar-Rajfah, the earthquake, in others. The punishment of al-Aykah is called aẓ-Ẓullah, the canopy of cloud. The people of al-Aykah were first struck by intense heat in their town, which nearly roasted them. Then a dense cloud came over the nearby forest and shaded all of it. Drawn by the shade and the cool breeze, all the people of the town gathered under the cloud. By Allah's arrangement, the criminals walked on their own two feet to the very spot where they were to die, with no warrant of arrest and no gun at their backs. Once they were all there, the cloud rained fire and an earthquake shook the ground, killing them all.

Other commentators say the people of Madyan and the people of al-Aykah were one people, and the three punishments struck them together. First came fire from the cloud, then with it a piercing blast, and then the earthquake shook the earth. This view has been preferred. Whether they were two peoples or one people with two names, what matters is the message of truth Shuʿayb brought them.

Another account says that Madyan was a son of Ibrāhīm by his third wife, Qaṭūrā. His descendants settled on the Arabian coast of the Red Sea. They believed in Allah and claimed to follow Ibrāhīm's religion. But five hundred years after Ibrāhīm they fell into wrong ways. They were a trading people, so their wrongdoing showed in their dealings. They kept no honesty in weights, measures and transactions.

### What do the two kinds of rights demand?

The essence of Islam, the shared call of all the blessed prophets, is the fulfilment of rights. Rights are of two kinds. Some belong directly to Allah, and no visible human gain or loss seems to hang on them, such as ṣalāh and ṣawm. Others are the rights of Allah's servants (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād), which concern people. Shuʿayb's people ignored both and acted against both.

By not believing in Allah and His messengers they violated the rights of Allah. By cutting weights and measures they sliced away at people's rights. On top of that they would sit at the entrances to roads and streets, terrorising travellers, robbing them, and threatening worse if they believed in Shuʿayb. So on Allah's good earth they made disorder the order of the day. Shuʿayb was sent to correct these misdeeds, and he told them three things: worship Allah alone, accept the clear proof, and deal fairly.

### Is short-changing only about scales?

Giving short weight and measure is forbidden, and so is cutting back on anyone's rights. Attacking someone's honour, failing to give someone the respect his rightful station deserves, falling short in obeying those who must be obeyed, and failing to honour those who must be honoured all fall under the crime Shuʿayb's people committed. In his famous sermon (khuṭbah) at the Farewell Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ declared that people's honour is as sacred and inviolable as their blood. That broadly confirms this view.

All of this comes under the Qur'an's words muṭaffifīn and taṭfīf, cheating in measure, wherever they occur. Allah says:

> "Woe to the defrauders! Those who take full measure ˹when they buy˺ from people, but give less when they measure or weigh for buyers. Do such people not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day—" (83:1-5).

The passage closes with "the Day ˹all˺ people will stand before the Lord of all worlds" (83:6).

These verses carry a stern warning and a sure promise, from which we ask Allah to save us. Al-Fārūq al-Aʿẓam once saw a man rushing through his bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration. He told him he had given short measure, meaning he had not given the prayer its due. Imam Mālik recorded this report. In that report, falling short in the prayer is itself called taṭfīf.

Allah has made the world run on perfect justice. In it there is no such thing as taking more from others and giving less in return. Everything works by justice, down to mathematical exactness. Unfair dealing goes against the balanced order (iṣlāḥ) that Allah has set, and it disturbs His well-balanced world.

### Why was Shuʿayb called the orator of the prophets?

Shuʿayb was known for his powerful speech, for which he was called the Orator of the Prophets, or Speaker of the Prophets, a title earned by the eloquence of his words and his counsel. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ also records this title. His address to his people continues in the verses that follow.

### In short

- Allah sent Shuʿayb, descended from Ibrāhīm through Madyan, to the people of Madyan and al-Aykah.
- He called them to worship Allah alone, to accept the clear proof, and to give full measure and weight.
- The ban on short-changing covers every right, of property, honour, respect and even the due of prayer.
- Corrupting the earth after Allah set it right breaks both its physical and its spiritual order.
- Honesty is better for them in both worlds, bringing Allah's reward and trust in the market.

86.text:
The Prophet Shuʿayb goes on to forbid his people the roadblocks they set up: "And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number. And consider the fate of the corruptors". When the people of Midian went to extremes in their wrongdoing, Shuʿayb urged them to be righteous and honest in their dealings. He made the need for honesty plain with clear arguments. But they would not accept his warning, and they would not accept his mission either. They twisted his teaching and spread misunderstandings about him among the people. They even turned to violence to stop people from supporting him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And do not lie in ambush on every road"**: do not sit in wait on every route that people use.

**"threatening"**: threatening travellers with death unless they handed over their money, for they were highway robbers, according to as-Suddī. Others say they beat and frightened strangers and stripped them of their clothes, or seized their garments, or charged them excise taxes. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and several others said it means threatening the believers who came to Shuʿayb to follow him. The first meaning is better, because Shuʿayb first speaks of "every road" and only then mentions the second matter.

**"and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path"**: barring from the path of Allah, His religion and obedience to Him, those who believed in Shuʿayb (Jethro) or wanted guidance, threatening to kill them.

**"and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked."** You want the path of Allah to look twisted and turned aside, other than it is, so that people will not follow it.

**"Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number."** You were weak because you were few, and later you became mighty through your great numbers. So remember Allah's favour and be thankful.

**"And consider the fate of the corruptors"**: look at the earlier nations and generations who spread corruption on the earth. See the torment and punishment they suffered for disobeying Allah and denying His messengers, and how their story ended in destruction and ruin.

### Was it one crime or two?

Some commentators say the two phrases, "threatening" and "hindering", carry the same sense. On this view the people stopped and threatened those who came to Shuʿayb, and that is what they were told not to do.

Others say these were two separate crimes. They sat on the highways looting and snatching people's goods, and they also stopped people from believing in Shuʿayb. So the first phrase describes the first crime and the second phrase the other. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and other works rely on this second view.

### Does the ban reach unlawful road tolls?

This command against robbery and extortion also covers checkpoints set up on roads to collect taxes that the Sharīʿah does not permit. ʿAllāmah al-Qurṭubī said that those who sit on highways and make people pay undue taxes against the Sharīʿah are criminals like Shuʿayb's people. Indeed, they are more oppressive and tyrannical than those people were.

### What does "seeking crookedness" mean?

These people were always looking for something on the path of Allah that they could twist, turn and misrepresent. From it they drew up their lists of doubts and objections, hoping to lure people away from the true religion.

### Why remind them of their numbers and of others' fate?

Shuʿayb used both encouragement and warning. The encouragement was the reminder of Allah's blessing. He had turned their small numbers into a large nation, or their economic weakness into wealth that needed no one. The warning was the call to look at the sad end of the peoples who had spread disorder on the earth. The peoples of Nūḥ (Noah), ʿĀd, Thamūd and Lūṭ (Lot) were examples of so many different punishments. Their fate should help Shuʿayb's people understand their own position and correct it.

### In short

- Shuʿayb forbade his people to lie in wait on the roads, robbing travellers and threatening those who came to believe in him.
- The command also covers unlawful tolls on roads. Al-Qurṭubī counted those who levy them among the worst oppressors.
- They sought to twist Allah's path and raise doubts so that people would turn from it.
- He reminded them how Allah had multiplied them, and warned them by the fate of Nūḥ's people, ʿĀd, Thamūd and Lūṭ's people.

87.text:
Shuʿayb answers a doubt that troubled his people: "If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with while others do not, then be patient until Allah judges between us. He is the Best of Judges.”" His people had split into two groups. Some believed in his call, and others went on rejecting him. Yet outwardly there was no difference between them, and both groups lived in comfort. If disbelief and denial were a crime, they reasoned, the criminals would surely have been punished.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with"**: some of you have indeed accepted the message my Lord gave me.

**"while others do not"**: and another group who do not believe in it.

**"then be patient"**: wait and see, O deniers, and do not be hasty.

**"until Allah judges between us."** Until Allah judges between us and you, by rescuing those who affirm this truth and destroying those who deny it. Then it will be clear who was on the path of truth and who were the liars. Those on the path of truth will be saved, and the liars will be destroyed.

**"He is the Best of Judges.”"** He is the fairest of judges. The happy outcome belongs to the God-fearing and obedient, and destruction to the disbelievers.

### Why does punishment not come at once?

The answer to their doubt was: do not be in a hurry. Allah is Forbearing and Merciful. He gives wrongdoers respite, and His decree comes into force only when they become utterly wicked and high-handed. Their present state was like that. If they held on to their denial, the time was not far off when the decisive punishment would overtake the deniers.

### In short

- Shuʿayb's people asked why believers and deniers lived equally well if denial was a crime.
- He told them to wait patiently, because Allah would judge between the two groups.
- Allah in His forbearance gives wrongdoers time. His decisive judgement comes when their wickedness is complete.

88.text:
Shuʿayb's people had argued that if he were truthful, his believers would be prospering and those who rejected him would be suffering, yet both sides lived comfortably, so how could he be true? He told them not to be hasty, for Allah would soon decide between the two groups. Unconvinced, the arrogant chiefs said what oppressive and arrogant people always say: "The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened, “O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.” He replied, “Even if we hate it". They threatened him and those who believed in him with exile from their town, or a forced return to the religion of the disbelievers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened"**: the leaders and important people who were too proud to believe.

**"“O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land"**: we will drive you out of our town, you and those who believe in you. The chiefs addressed these words to the Messenger Shuʿayb, but meant those who followed his religion too.

**"unless you return to our faith.”"** Unless you all come back to our religion and our old way of life and worship.

**"He replied, “Even if we hate it"**: will you compel us, though we loathe what you invite us to and know the falsehood beneath it? He said this in astonishment. The question is a refusal. In effect: are you telling us to return to your faith even though we dislike it and know it to be false? It is a way of saying that this can never happen.

### Why "return" to a faith Shuʿayb never held?

It is easy to see why they told the believers to "return" to their old faith. All of them had once been part of the disbelievers' religion and way of life, and had accepted Islam only later. But Shuʿayb's case was different. He had never followed their false faith for a single day. No prophet of Allah could ever follow a faith opposed to pure monotheism. So why would they tell him to return to it?

Perhaps before he was given prophethood, Shuʿayb kept silent about their false words and deeds and lived among them as one of them. So his disbelieving people took him for one of their own, a fellow-traveller who shared their faith. Only when he called them to true īmān did they discover that his religion was different from theirs. That led them to conclude that he had left their old faith.

There is also a point of grammar. In addressing Shuʿayb, the plural, which covers his followers, outweighs the singular, because Shuʿayb himself had never belonged to their religious community. And Shuʿayb answered in the plural in the same way.

### In short

- The arrogant chiefs threatened to exile Shuʿayb and the believers unless they returned to the old religion.
- The threat was aimed at his followers too, who had once shared that religion.
- Shuʿayb had never followed their faith, but before his prophethood they had taken him for one of them.
- His reply, "Even if we hate it?", is a firm refusal to go back to what they knew was false.

89.text:
Shuʿayb completes his answer: "We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”" Allah had saved them from the false faith. Going back to it now would be a grave and false accusation against Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith"**: if we followed your disbelief and polytheism, joining partners with Allah as rivals to Him, we would be uttering a tremendous lie against Him.

**"after Allah has saved us from it."** He rescued us from your religion by His grace.

**"It does not befit us to return to it"**: it is not right or permissible for us to adopt your false religion of associating others with Allah.

**"unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord."** Unless Allah wills it and abandons us to it, or, as one explanation puts it, unless He takes away the knowledge from our hearts. We will do whatever He wills. These words refer every matter to Allah's will.

**"Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge."** His knowledge embraces all things, including my situation and yours. He has perfect knowledge of every matter, and His watch covers everything. So He knows what is right for His servants, and nothing is hidden from Him.

**"In Allah we trust."** We rely on Allah alone in all our affairs, in what we do and what we leave. He will keep us firm on the right path and guard us from the ways that lead to Hell.

**"Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth."** Decide between us and our people with justice. Grant us victory over them, and support the people of truth and the oppressed against those who oppress. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the word fatḥ here means "decide". That is how fātiḥ comes to mean a judge (qāḍī).

**"You are the best of those who judge.”"** You are the Most Just, who never wrongs anyone in His judgement.

### Why would returning be a lie against Allah?

First, to give kufr and shirk the status of a faith implies that Allah commanded them, and that is inventing a lie against Him. Second, to return to disbelief after believing in the revealed truth (īmān), and after gaining knowledge and insight into it, would mean saying that the first way was false and the later one true. That is plainly a double lie and slander: taking the true (ḥaqq) for false (bāṭil), and the false for true.

### Why add "unless Allah wills"?

Shuʿayb's words "we can never return to your religion" carried a hint of self-assertion. Outwardly at least, such a claim does not fit the selfless submission (ʿabdiyyah) of a true servant of Allah. It does not suit those who are near to Allah and know Him. So he added, "unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust."

This sentence mirrors his humility (ʿajz), his trust in Allah (tawakkul) and his confident handing over of every matter to Him (tafwīḍ). These are the master virtues of the prophets. In effect he says: who are we to say that we will do something or keep away from something? The ability to do good and to keep away from evil is nothing but Allah's grace. The Prophet ﷺ said the same: had it not been for Allah's grace, they would not have been guided, nor given in charity, nor prayed.

### Why did Shuʿayb turn to prayer?

Because he trusted Allah alone, Shuʿayb realised after speaking with the arrogant chiefs that nothing would move them. So he stopped addressing them and made his duʿāʾ to Allah: "Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth." Through these words Shuʿayb was in fact praying for the destruction of the disbelievers among his people. Allah answered his prayer, and they were destroyed by an earthquake.

### Why was a believing people destroyed for dishonesty?

When Allah's punishment came, the people of Midian were destroyed. In Allah's eyes, respecting the rights of fellow human beings and honesty in dealings matter so much that a community was destroyed despite claiming to be believers. Allah is the best Judge, and His judgement is never biased.

### In short

- Returning to the old religion would be a double lie against Allah, calling shirk a faith and calling the truth false.
- Shuʿayb tempered his refusal with "unless Allah wills", showing the humility, trust and surrender that mark the prophets.
- Doing good and avoiding evil come only by Allah's grace, as the Prophet ﷺ taught.
- When words had no effect, Shuʿayb asked Allah to judge between them. His prayer was answered with the earthquake that destroyed the deniers.

90.text:
Allah shows how deep the disbelief, rebellion and defiance of Shuʿayb's people ran: "The disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened, “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!”" It was a misleading statement by the arrogant chiefs, said among themselves or to their followers, as Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ reports from ʿAṭāʾ.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened"**: the leaders and important people who refused the call to believe in Allah's oneness. Some of them said it to others, and they said it to the lowly among the people, warning them against Shuʿayb and his faith. They swore it, for in the Arabic la-in, "if", carries the lām of an oath.

**"“If you follow Shu’aib"**: if you follow his religion and his way, and leave the way of life of our ancestors.

**"you will surely be losers!”"** You will be ignorant dupes and will certainly come to ruin.

### What was their real crime?

Shuʿayb's people were not guilty of denying Allah. Their guilt was misrepresenting Him. They credited to Allah a religion He had never sent. This has been the position of the peoples of all the prophets. They were no different from those to whom Allah had earlier revealed His religion. But by their own changes and additions they turned it into something else. They made Allah's religion into the religion of their desires and went on calling it Allah's religion.

The religious leaders of such a time, backed by the people and holding power, know they cannot win an argument with a prophet. Yet they do not want anyone to rob them of their importance, so they look for a way to silence him. The chiefs' threat to their own followers was exactly such a way.

### In short

- The disbelieving chiefs swore to their people that following Shuʿayb would bring them ruin.
- Their real guilt was claiming that a religion of their own making came from Allah.
- Unable to answer a prophet, such leaders try to silence him and frighten others away.

91.text:
The punishment came for their threat to drive out Shuʿayb and his followers: "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes". Here the punishment is called an earthquake (rajfah, zalzalah). Other verses describe it in other words.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them"**: the violent quake seized them, together with the loud cry announcing their punishment.

**"and they fell lifeless in their homes"**: in the morning they lay dead in their dwellings, their town and their encampments, fallen on their knees and faces.

### How do the different descriptions fit together?

Allah mentions their end again in Sūrah Hūd:

> "When Our command came, We saved Shu’aib and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us. And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes" (11:94).

That verse mentions the blast because they had mocked Shuʿayb, saying, "Does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our forefathers worshipped" (11:87). So it was fitting to mention the cry that silenced them, after they had mocked his ṣalāh. In Sūrat ash-Shuʿarāʾ, Allah says, "So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud" (26:189). That was because they had challenged Shuʿayb: "So cause ˹deadly˺ pieces of the sky to fall upon us, if what you say is true" (26:187).

So all these forms of punishment struck them on the Day of the Cloud, Yawm aẓ-Ẓullah. First came a dark cloud over them, holding fire, flames and a terrible light. Then a cry came down from the sky, and a tremor shook them from beneath. Their souls were taken, their lives ended and their bodies lay still.

### What did Ibn ʿAbbās say about the day of the cloud?

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās explained how the earthquake and the cloud came together, as Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ records. First a heat fell on them so fierce that it was as though a door of Hell had opened toward them. They could not breathe, and neither shade nor water gave relief. They went down into cellars, but it was hotter there. With nowhere left to turn, they fled the city for the nearby forest. There Allah sent a thick cloud, with a cool breeze beneath it. Half-crazed by the heat, they all rushed into its shade. Then the whole cloud turned to fire and rained down on them, and the earthquake came too and reduced them to ashes. So the punishment of the earthquake and the punishment of the cloud fell on them at the same time.

Some commentators suggest another possibility: that Shuʿayb's people were in separate groups, some struck by the earthquake and others destroyed by the cloud. The question of whether Madyan and al-Aykah were one people or two was discussed under 7:85.

### In short

- The earthquake struck Shuʿayb's people for threatening to expel him and the believers, and they lay dead in their homes.
- Other verses speak of a blast and of the day of the cloud. These match their mockery of his prayer and their dare to bring down the sky.
- Ibn ʿAbbās described unbearable heat, a flight to a shaded forest, and a cloud that rained fire as the earth shook.

92.text:
This verse presents the fate of Shuʿayb's people as a lesson, which is the real purpose of telling the story: "Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there. Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers". The very people who threatened to drive the believers out were the ones who lost everything.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there."** One meaning of the Arabic word ghinā is to live somewhere in peace and comfort, and that is the meaning here. The homes where they had lived in ease became so desolate after the punishment that it was as if comfort had never been there. They were all destroyed. It looked as though they had never lived in the land from which they had wanted to expel their messenger Shuʿayb and his followers.

Grammatically, "those who rejected Shuʿayb" (alladhīna kadhdhabū Shuʿayban) is the subject. Its predicate is introduced by "as if" (ka-an), a softened form of ka-annahum, "as if they", with its subject left unstated.

**"Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers"**: they were the losers, punished, losing themselves and their possessions. The believers lost nothing at all, contrary to what the disbelievers had claimed. Repeating "those who rejected Shuʿayb" serves to refute what they had said before: "If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!" (7:90). They threatened to throw Shuʿayb and his believing companions out of their city, but in the end the loss fell on no one but themselves.

### When does a people lose all claim to mercy?

Allowances can be made for a person as long as the truth is not clear to him. But once the truth has been made clear and he still chooses arrogance, he loses any claim to sympathy. Punishment in this world is given on this basis. On the same basis, people's punishment in the Hereafter will be decided according to their guilt.

### In short

- Shuʿayb's people were wiped out so completely that it was as if they had never lived in comfort in their homes.
- Those who threatened to expel the believers, warning that following Shuʿayb meant loss, turned out to be the real losers.
- Once the truth is clear, persisting in arrogance forfeits all sympathy, in this world and the next.

93.text:
After the punishment fell, the Prophet Shuʿayb turned from his people with words of reproach: "He turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”" He had delivered everything he was sent with. Since they disbelieved in what he brought, he would not grieve for them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He turned away from them"**: when the punishment was about to fall on his people, Shuʿayb and his believing companions moved away from that place. One explanation says he left them before they were destroyed. Others say he turned from them once they had been destroyed. Most commentators say these blessed people went to Makkah and stayed there until the end of their lives.

**"saying, “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord"**: I conveyed to you what my Lord told me to convey, explaining His commands and prohibitions.

**"and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice."** I warned you of Allah's punishment and invited you to repent and believe. But you did not take my advice or follow my guidance.

**"How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”"** Why should I grieve over a people who disbelieved in Allah, insisted on their disbelief and were destroyed for it? The question is rhetorical and means: I will not grieve.

### Why did a prophet speak like this?

Shuʿayb had prayed that his people be chastened, out of utter disappointment with people sunk in disobedience and stubbornness. But when the punishment actually came as a result, his heart ached, out of a prophet's care and love for his people. So it was to calm his own heart that he spoke these words to them. He had done all that was required of him, and the loss was theirs.

### In short

- After the punishment, Shuʿayb and the believers left, most say for Makkah, where they lived out their days.
- He reminded his destroyed people that he had delivered his Lord's messages and advised them sincerely.
- His words calmed his own grieving heart, since those who chose disbelief had brought their end on themselves.

94.text:
After the stories of earlier peoples comes a general rule, a warning for people now, so that they may escape the fate of those before them: "Whenever We sent a prophet to a society, We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled". The ruin described so far was not limited to the peoples of Nūḥ (Noah), ʿĀd and Thamūd. It is Allah's usual way to send prophets to guide people to lasting success. When a people ignores their counsel and rejects their call, Allah sends hardship upon it, hoping it will come back to Him in repentance. This verse (7:94) states the first half of the rule, and the next (7:95) gives the second.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whenever We sent a prophet to a society"**: whenever Allah sent a messenger to a town whose people denied him, and whose people He later destroyed.

**"We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity"**: the words are baʾsāʾ and ḍarrāʾ. One explanation says baʾsāʾ means the physical illnesses and ailments they suffered, and ḍarrāʾ the poverty and humiliation they went through. Another says baʾsāʾ means hunger or poverty and ḍarrāʾ means illness. The Qur'an uses the words in these senses elsewhere too, and ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd confirmed these meanings. Some linguists say baʾsāʾ is financial hardship and ḍarrāʾ is loss of health. Others list fear, affliction and hardship, and illness, pain and hunger. All this came before their destruction.

**"so perhaps they would be humbled"**: so that they might call on Allah, humble themselves before Him and ask Him to remove their afflictions. Then they might lay aside their pride and disbelief and come to believe. But they did not do what He commanded. This was a warning for Quraysh and for every people who disbelieve and reject Allah's way.

### Why does the Qur'an tell history this way?

So far the surah has told the stories of five earlier prophets and their peoples. The sixth, the story of Mūsā (Moses) and his people, comes a few verses later. The Qur'an's way with history differs from that of history books. It does not try to give an event in full or in strict order. It picks out the part that matters and stresses the lesson it holds.

### Why does Allah send hardship?

It is human nature to turn to the Creator in distress. So this suffering is really a blessing from Allah in disguise, meant for people's good. The great spiritual guide Maulānā Rūmī put it in verse: people are made to treat you badly so that you will turn to your Lord in tears.

Allah sends all kinds of difficulty on people so that their hearts may soften and they may stop relying on anything other than Him. Their arrogance, which keeps them from accepting truth from outside themselves, may then shrink. In this way, by Allah's arrangement, a sense of one's own shortcomings and helplessness is planted in a person, so that he gives the voice of truth his full attention. Both the general public and those to whom a prophet is sent go through this treatment.

But by Allah's usual way, all of this comes wrapped in doubt. When trouble strikes someone, it comes through the ordinary chain of cause and effect. That is what makes it a test for so many people. They dismiss it, saying it was bound to happen, and it did.

### In short

- Whenever a people rejected their prophet, Allah first struck them with hardship, illness and poverty, so that they might humble themselves.
- Such hardship is a mercy in disguise, meant to soften hearts and break the pride that blocks the truth.
- Because hardship comes through ordinary causes, many dismiss it as chance and miss its lesson.
- The Qur'an tells history selectively, for its lessons, and this rule is a warning to Quraysh and every later people.

95.text:
When the first test failed, Allah tested them in the opposite way: "Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.” So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware". They had been put through hardship so that they would repent and turn to Allah. When they learnt nothing from it, they were given the test of ease.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then We changed their adversity to prosperity"**: the word sayyiʾah here means distress, and ḥasanah means prosperity. Allah replaced hardship with ease, sickness with health and well-being, and poverty with plentiful provision. Drought and failed fruit gave way to fertile land, abundance and comfort, so that they might thank Allah for it. But they did none of this.

**"until they flourished"**: the word ʿafaw means they increased and grew in numbers, wealth and children, and in strength.

**"and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.”"** Out of ingratitude for this grace, they said: hardship and happiness came to our fathers before us, just as they have come to us. This is only the way of time, not something from Allah, so hold firm to what you follow. In effect: our fathers suffered hardship and distress as we have, yet they held to their religion, and we are like them and will follow their example. They meant to say that their suffering and their prosperity had nothing to do with their deeds. It was simply the natural turn of events, a cycle in which sometimes we suffer hardship and sometimes we enjoy plenty.

**"So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware"**: Allah struck them with punishment all at once, while they had no idea it was coming and did not expect it. That came after they stubbornly persisted in their evil and ignorance.

### Why did they fail both tests?

Allah tested them with hardship and then with ease and plenty, so that they might humble themselves and turn to Him. But they failed both tests. Neither one moved them to change their ways. They did not grasp Allah's wisdom, or the fact that He was testing them in both states.

When hardship does not teach people, Allah changes their conditions for the better. Then they fall into a worse misunderstanding. They feel sure that all this is just the way of the times, the usual ups and downs people go through. Otherwise, they reason, good days would not have followed bad ones. So they learn nothing from either set of circumstances. Prosperity granted to people who have behaved arrogantly is a grave danger sign. It is a sign that Allah has decided to seize the guilty at the very point where he feels most secure from His punishment.

The real reward of a life of fearing Allah comes in the Hereafter. Yet if Allah wills, He gives a first instalment of it in this world too, in the form of well-being and honour.

### How does a believer face good and bad times?

Believers, by contrast, thank Allah in good times and are patient in hard times. A hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ says the believer's affair is amazing, for whatever Allah decrees for him is good for him. If harm (ḍarrāʾ) strikes him, he is patient, and that is good for him. If he is given ease, he thanks Allah, and that too is good for him. So the believer understands that both prosperity and adversity are tests from Allah.

Another hadith says that the believer will go on being tested with afflictions until he comes out pure of sin. The hypocrite, by contrast, is like a donkey that does not know why its owners tied it up or why they let it go.

### What does sudden seizure mean?

"So We seized them by surprise" describes punishment coming all at once. A hadith about sudden death says it is a mercy for the believer, but a punishment that brings regret for the disbeliever.

### In short

- When hardship did not humble them, Allah gave them health, wealth and growing numbers as a second test.
- They called both hardship and ease mere cycles of fate, like those their forefathers had known, and so learnt from neither.
- Prosperity after arrogance is a warning sign, and Allah seized them suddenly when they felt most secure.
- A believer is patient in hardship and grateful in ease, and so gains from both.
